subtopic: EXPIRY OF UNITED STATES LEGISLATION- RETENTION OF CANADIAN CONTROLS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: EXPIRY OF UNITED STATES LEGISLATION- RETENTION OF CANADIAN CONTROLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might give the house a little information with respect to the matters of price control in the United States and the attitude of this government towards the possible consequences thereof.
On June 30, the emergency legislation in the United States which authorized price, rent and rationing controls expired. As I understand it, the consequence is that there is at the present time under federal law no price control, no rent control and, with the possible exception of sugar, no rationing in the United States. There are, of course, certain states and municipalities which have taken emergency measures or maintained existing regulations which are not affected by the. expiration of the federal law.
This situation has, not unnaturally, raised certain questions in the minds of many Canadians. The government feels that the first opportunity should be taken to assure parliament and the country that there is no intention of abandoning similar controls in Canada.

Foreign Exchange Control
Developments affecting prices in other countries, particularly the United States, are, of course, not without their effect upon Canada. Our policies have, in the past, and will, in the future, necessarily continue to have such developments in mind.
Price control, rent control and the control of supplies existed in Canada before they were adopted in the United States. Canadian regulations, while similar in objective to those in the United States, have often differed quite widely both as to their form and their nature. In other words, we in Canada have followed our own course, which we believe is well adapted to Canadian conditions and to the Canadian economy. We shall continue to follow policies which we believe to be in the general interest, making, from time to time, such modifications as seem to be required in the light of internal and external conditions as they develop.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the suggestion of the minister and I wish to make just one or two brief comments.
This bill is one of very great importance, not only because of the matters contained in it, but because I think it is another step towards the further control of our lives by experts. Now experts are very good poeple, and in the last several years we have had to submit to them in many ways, and we are not going to get rid of that for some time. But I do feel that in considering a bill of this kind we should bear in mind its far-reaching implications, and that it is, whether we wish it or not, another step to a controlled economy.
In particular I want to make one suggestion, which can be further considered in the committee, but I am making it now in the hope that possibly it may not become a matter of party difference. The suggestion I make is that this bill should not be made of indefinite tenure, but that it should be for a limited period. The emergency powers bill was for a limited period, and I suggest it would be very desirable that this bill be for a limited period, for this particular reason: if it extends for an indefinite time it just goes on and on, and people get used to the idea, and there is no opportunity for it to be reviewed. It becomes part of the landscape. I do suggest, and this is the only point on which I shall take up the time of the house, that the government might very seriously consider whether this bill, like the emergency powers bill, might not be made for a special period. Then it could, if necessary, be extended. That would have two results. First of all, the act will have to come up and justify itself. Secondly, and perhaps most important, if it is for a special period, then those in charge of its administration will almost automatically have moral pressure put upon them to try during that period to work towards a situation where it may no longer be necessary to continue it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few comments to make regarding the general principle and purpose of the bill, because after all we do endorse the principle on second reading. On the resolution stage, on June 17 last, I stated that this group believed it would be in the interest of Canada to maintain the foreign exchange control board as a peacetime measure. We believe that the board served this country well during the war, and that it can have a very important part to play in the future. But when I said that I made it quite clear that I did not mean that in supporting the principle we approved all the policies of the board in the past or as it operates to-day.
There is one statement in the preamble which I would like to read, and then explain the situation with regard to it. At line 13 of the preamble we find the statement:
And whereas it is desirable to provide means for achieving orderly exchange arrangements and in general discharging the obligations of Canada as a member of the international monetary fund.
When the Bretton Woods agreement was before the house for discussion last year, I think we of this group made it quite clear that we were opposed to that agreement. However, parliament decided , that we should become a member of the international monetary fund, and also of the bank of reconstruction. A sufficient number of other nations agreed to join the fund, and therefore it is understood that we are going ahead with the Bretton Woods agreement, and that the machinery for the fund, and the bank, are being set up. That being so, although we are still of the same opinion, that it would be a good thing for the world at large if the Bretton Woods agreement were dropped, nevertheless, in view of the fact that it is being gone on with, we think it important that everything possible should be done to make the fund work in the interests of Canada and of the world as a whole. But we emphasize the view that we should be

very careful not to sign any more agreements which will still further restrict the action of the foreign exchange control board. In saying that I have especially in mind the United States proposals for expansion of international trade.	.
We are convinced that the Bretton Woods agreement will not prove a success unless the creditor nations are prepared to make far-reaching changes in their trade policies. Unfortunately there does not seem to be any sign on the part of the creditor nations that they intend to make those changes. The Minister of Finance, in his speech on June 17, seemed very uncertain regarding the future condition of international affairs. He seemed to have grave doubts in his mind as to just what was going to happen. I should like to quote his remarks in that regard, to be found on page 2547 of Hansard:
I should like to summarize what I have said in this way. The general character of the international financial and economic relations between nations which is going to prevail in the future is still uncertain. We hope that it will be one which does not call for restrictive controls and we shall do evertyhing in our power to bring this about. But we cannot be certain that the world we are going into will be what we would like to see. It may be a world of economic friction instead of cooperation.
I should like to pause there to say that I wonder whether if the minister thinks that capitalizing on the distress of certain nations resulting from the war, to force those nations into adverse, even suicidal agreements such as that of Bretton Woods, will help to remove that friction I wonder whether the minister really thinks that to force nations into these agreements helps to establish good will, restore confidence and prevent the development of the kind of friction which he seems to be afraid of. I would further ask whether the discussions which have already taken place between the United States and Great Britain on the proposed loan have helped to increase good will between those nations. I believe everyone who has read the discussions which have taken place about it in the United States and Britain must agree that the situation has been further aggravated and more friction has developed. I proceed with the minister's speech:
We cannot demobilize our main economic defence without being absolutely certain that it will not be needed. We cannot leave ourselves in a position where our choice of domestic economic policies has to be influenced by the consideration that one policy or another may lead to capital withdrawal by foreigners or capital flight by Canadians.
Let me say here that if that is true of Canada, as a gold producer and as a nation which in the past has been able to maintain a favourable balance of payments for a number

of years, how much more true must it be of those nations which are not gold producers and have had the experience of a chronic unbalance of trade in the past.
But the next statement of the minister is one to which I particularly wish to draw the attention of the house, because it appears to be a very peculiar statement to make at this time:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movement.
This is the point I want to refer to:
We expect to be able to avoid any interference with current account transactions.
Why should the minister say that we expect to avoid any interference with current account transactions? He knows very well that by the Bret ton Woods agreement we have to avoid it whether we like it or not; we have no power under the agreement to interfere with current accounts; therefore why does he say that we expect to be able to avoid this interference? Is he starting now to doubt whether we can carry out the Bretton Woods agreement?

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance was under the impression that we would be protected under article VII, which provides that when a scarcity of currency develops we are allowed to place restrictions against the imports of nations whose currency is scarce. But unfortunately article VII applies only when a scarcity of currency develops in the fund; it does not apply when a scarcity of currency develops within any one nation. The mere development of scarcity of currency within one nation does not permit that nation to place a restriction against the imports of the nation whose currency is scarce.
The minister in his speech proceeded to emphasize the need for the stabilization of exchange. But I think he must be careful not to confuse effect with cause. Fluctuations in rates of exchange, apart from speculation, are very largely the effect of adverse trade balances. Nations in the past have devalued their currencies in order to expand exports and thereby balance their trade. The monetary fund definitely limits that pow-er under articles IV, V and VI, and under article VI proceeds to penalize a nation which is unable to balance its trade over a period of time.
Take the position of Canada prior to the war, and again to-day. The minister refers to it on page 2540 of Hansard. He states:
With the United Kingdom, the rest of the sterling area, and with the continent of Europe, we had a surplus; with the United States wo had a deficit.
Surely the logical solution of a condition of that kind would be an attempt to expand our imports from the United Kingdom and the rest of the sterling area, in order to make it possible for them to balance their trade with us, and either expand our exports to the United States, or, if they refused to buy, curtail our imports. Unfortunately, however, we no longer have that power. Under the Bretton Woods agreement we have given up that power, so that we are unable to restrict imports from a nation which insists upon having a favourable balance of trade with us. Under the United States proposals for the expansion of trade, that power will be still further restricted. Of course, so far as I understand it, Canada has not signed the United States proposals. Britain was forced to sign them in order to get her loan, and I think it is generally understood that Canada intends to sign as well. But again I say that if we want to make the Bretton Woods agreement succeed we should be very careful not to place any further handicaps on our foreign exchange control board.
While the minister refers to the fact that, under article VII, when a currency becomes scarce the nations are allowed to place restrictions against imports, on the other hand the nation which everyone has in mind when talking about scarce currency is, of course, the United States of America. Personally I am very doubtful indeed whether the United States will allow her currency to become scarce, because if she were to allow a scarcity of her currency with the fund, then the nations of the world would be allowed to place restrictions against imports from the United States. It is far more likely that the United States will expand her loans to other countries, or buy gold, thereby preventing her currency from becoming scarce in the fund, and thereby preventing other countries from exercising any controls or restrictions whatsoever against imports from her. Of course, by making loans, they gradually buy up the capital assets of the debtor nations, and you have a vicious form of American imperialism in operation.
One of our main complaints against these proposals is that they do not provide in reality for the stabilization of the currency at its real value, but merely in terms of gold; because no provision whatsoever is made in the Bretton Woods agreement- or in the United States proposals for the stabilization of price levels. And of course the real value of money must be based upon the purchasing power

In order that Britain may meet her obligations under the Bretton Woods agreement and under her loan from America, we are told that she has to expand her exports by seventy-five per cent. We are entering into competition with Britain for markets in Latin-America, and we are also trying to expand our exports. That is bound to result in keen competition. With that kind of policy I am not surprised that the minister states he views with some alarm the kind of world which may be developing, because Canada is taking an active part in helping to develop international friction. The statement goes on:
Markets must be found for $1,750,000,000 to $2,000,000,000 worth of exports if Canada is to maintain employment and income at desirable levels, according to the opinions of dominion economists.
The United States is expected to continue, in the long run, as Canada's best peace-time customer. The United Kingdom, which formerly tied sometimes with the United States for first place in Canadian trade, -will be unable to approach her pre-war purchasing rate unless pending loans from the United States and the dominion are approved.

And the information was supplied, I suppose, either by the Department of Trade and Commerce or by some confident-

ial source. I will not suggest that any official secrets have been disclosed. By way of comment on it I would say that the only way Britain can expand her trade and meet her obligations is by Canada and the United States buying more goods from Britain. Apparently we are not so much interested in that as we are in expanding our exports, because time and again the Minister of Finance has stated in this house that we shall use large amounts of our sterling balances not for the purpose of buying more goods from Britain but in order to meet obligations to the United States. One wonders just how Britain will be able to meet her obligations if the United States adopts the same tactics.
I was quite interested in a Canadian press dispatch which appeared in the papers under date of June 26. The heading of the article is:	"United States Opposition May Delay
Anglo-Canadian Wheat Pact", and it reads as follows:
United States opposition to the proposed Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement may delay negotiations but will not prevent an agreement being reached, officials in touch with diplomatic and market aspects of the question said to-day.

It was freely admitted, however, that the United States has presented to the Anglo-Canadian negotiators a number of factors that must be considered:
These are:
1.	The reaction in the United States if the purchase agreement enables Britain to buy wheat from Canada over a long period at a price little more than half that which American farmers are receiving.
I am specially interested in the next point:
2.	The inconsistency of such a bilateral agreement in the light of the white paper issued by the State Department last December and endorsed by Britain calling for an international effort to remove trading discriminations and put world commerce under control of multilateral agreements ensuring free opportunity to all.
It is understood the British negotiators, led by Food Minister John Strachey. were asked to consider what the effect of a bilateral agreement to purchase Canadian wheat would be on the congressional debate over approval of the $3,750,000,000 loan to Britain.
I read that because I am interested in the view expressed by officials of the United States, that they consider this agreement to be a contravention of the white paper. When we were discussing the Bretton Woods agreement last year we warned that by signing the agreement we would be making it difficult for Canada to make trade agreements with countries in Europe; that these trade agreements might be regarded by the United States as a contravention of the Bretton Woods agreement. Now when the first major agreement comes up, the United States apparently is objecting to it on the ground that Britain

Foreign Exchange Control
is breaking her obligations under the white paper. I take it that the white paper is not the Bretton Woods agreement but the United States proposals for expansion of world trade. Maybe that is the proposal which Britain signed, .but so far we have not signed it. But an agreement must be between two people; it cannot be on the part of one only. Therefore if the countries in Europe are bound by an international agreement with the United States, it becomes impossible for us to make a contract with them which is a violation of their agreement with the United States.
Another point I want to bring out is that we are asking the farmers at the present time to accept prices considerably lower than world market prices, on the understanding that we will have a long-term agreement for the future under which they will receive good prices. Now apparently we are finding it difficult to make these long-term agreements. Again I emphasize that we must be very careful, not to sign the United States proposals for an expansion of world trade until certain amendments have been made to those proposals.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext: We have signed too many already.

subtopic: STATUTORY AUTHORITY FOR ORDERS IN COUNCIL PASSED UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
Yes, but we do not want to make it worse by signing more. If anything, we should try to amend the existing agreements, though I know that is practically impossible. The important point is that control of foreign exchange should be for the purpose of helping to maintain the development of a nation's resources at an optimum level. As long as nations are willing to balance their trade, there need foe no difficulty in stabilizing the rates of foreign exchange. On the other hand when creditor nations refuse to accept payment in goods, thereby forcing other nations into debt, currency devaluation is bound to ensue as a necessary protection. That was one of our main complaints against the Bretton Woods agreement-that while it removed a nation's defence, it did not remove the causes which made a nation want to make use of that defence. Therefore I would say the consequence of the Bretton Woods agreement and of all these international agreements may very well be not an expansion of international trade but a reduction of imports and an intensification of economic nationalism. Already we are seeing that very thing take place in Great Britain; it has been referred to on more than one occasion by Prime Minister Attlee. He has spoken of the need to reduce imports in order to meet their foreign obligations, and the need to develop their own resources to a greater extent so that they will
not have to depend upon the resources of other nations. That is the attitude Britain is taking to-day after signing an agreement supposed to be for the purpose of expanding trade. Already in Britain it is having the effect of intensifying economic nationalism. So I would go so far as to say that the inevitable consequence of the operation of these various international control measures will be an intensification of economic nationalism, unless there is a complete change of policy on the part of the creditor nations, of which there is no sign at the present time.
Under the Bretton Woods agreement the Canadian dollar is to be valued in terms of the United States dollar or gold; and I understand it will be largely the responsibility of the foreign exchange control board to maintain, that relationship. Suggestions have been made by a number of people, and suggestions were made in this house on June 17, that it would be in the interests of Canada to maintain the Canadian dollar on a parity with the United States dollar. When the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), I think it was, made that suggestion on the 17th I stated that I did not think it would be to the advantage of Canada to maintain parity with the United States. Unfortunately at that time Hansard dropped the word " not," giving my words the opposite meaning; but on every occasion this matter has come up in the house I have objected to the suggestion that the Canadian dollar should be placed on a parity with the United States dollar. My reason for taking that position is this: If that parity is established, either Canadian exporters will receive ten per cent less for their exports or the foreign purchasers will pay ten per cent more. In either case Canadian exports will be discouraged; and in view of the fact that the United States is our main, or perhaps I should say our only, creditor, the present need is to encourage our exports to that country rather than the reverse. If we raise the value of the Canadian dollar, in terms of the United States dollar, by ten per cent, then under the Bretton Woods agreement our currency will be raised ten per cent in relation to the currency of all nations, not merely that of the United States, because all currencies are convertible under the Bretton Woods agreement. So our primary producers may be at a serious disadvantage in competing with nations such as Australia, the Argentine, New Zealand, and perhaps in the future Russia, because of the fact that their currencies are already depreciated considerably below the Canadian dollar. Moreover, Australia, Newr Zealand and Russia have not signed the Bretton Woods agreement; therefore in
Foreign Exchange Control

future they will be able to devalue their currency to any extent they see fit, while we, having signed the Bretton Woods agreement, would be able to devalue our currency only ten per cent below the rate set when we joined in the agreement. Therefore it does seem to me that as long as we are under the Bretton Woods agreement, which in my opinion represents nothing more or less than laissez-faire capitalism, cut-throat competition and American imperialism, we must protect ourselves by maintaining the Canadian dollar below the United States dollar, because once we set the value of the Canadian dollar we are allowed to vary it by only ten per cent one way or the other without the permission of the fund.
So let us hope the day will come when the creditor nations will recognize their responsibility to balance their trade. Then and only then, I believe, the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar with any other unit of currency can be established on the basis of the internal price level in Canada as compared with the corresponding price levels in other countries. Then one of the main causes of international friction and international trade restrictions will be eliminated, and international trade may help promote good will and friendship. Then perhaps the minister will be able to look to the future with less fear than he looks to it to-day.

The minister, speaking on his own behalf, although I am sure he shares the confidence of the cabinet, says that our dollar is the stronger dollar. Many of our industries, such as newsprint, find that the profit on their product, which is sold largely in the United States, depends upon the exchange. The United States dollar commands a premium now, and there might be great repercussions if we allowed our dollar to go to a premium over it.
This brings me to the point which I mentioned earlier, that I am quite willing that we should have control until we find out where we are going to be after Bretton Woods, which, as I understand it, will have to do with the setting of what the interrelationships of foreign exchanges are to be. Until that time let us continue it, because we may find that the Canadian dollar will not sell at ten per cent discount vis-a-vis the American dollar and ten per cent premium vis-a-vis sterling.
I should like to point to one or two considerations which are in my mind as we consider this bill, which is to be sent to the banking and commerce committee. First I should like to ask how much better off Canada would have been in 1939 than she was had we had foreign exchange controls during the thirties, with all the nuisance of the forms and regulations which foreign exchange control entails. The government of the day did a very good job in 1939 in clamping on the controls and freezing all capital movement and current account movement between Canada and other countries. We were thus able to conserve our currency, and subsequently by means of the Hyde Park agreement Canada was able to exercise a beneficial control over her international exchange account. How much better off would we have been had we had foreign exchange control prior to 1939? How much better off shall we be if we continue foreign exchange control now, with all the nuisances that accompany it, if at some future time an emergency such as a war should arise? Shall we be better off with that control than we would be if we allowed exchange to take its normal course, and clamp on the control when an emergency arises? It seems to me that if we maintain controls now, there is some validity in the comparison of a nation keeping a standing army in peace time. There are certain things a nation can afford and certain things it cannot afford because they are not worth while.
While there is relative freedom on current account as far as international trade is concerned, that is in anyone getting foreign exchange in order to purchase goods abroad, and also in selling foreign exchange which we receive for goods we have sold abroad- there is not much difficulty in connection with current account-on capital account transactions, however, there are definite restrictions. In other words if a Canadian wishes to make a new investment in the United States or some other country, he is prevented from doing so by the regulations now' in force.
May I just make an observation here which I think has some consequence. I do not think it is too much to say that the fact that Great Britain through her early history had a free capital market whereby her nationals could invest money anywhere in the world, the fact that she had built up a large foreign investment reserve, the fact that that reserve was available at the outbreak of the war before the United States adopted lend-lease and when Great Britain had to pay cash on the barrel head, saved civilization. I do not think it is an exaggeration to make that statement. It certainly gave Great Britain a chance to get goods and munitions to hold off the enemy and give the rest of us on this side of the Atlantic a chance to arm for the conflict.
While some reasons may be advanced why foreign exchange control on capital account should be maintained, I wonder if we fully understand the advantages of having a free capital market. If we were so unfortunate as to become engaged in another war and found that our nationals had large investments abroad, or across the border, we could realize on those investments and immediately get goods or munitions into our country' where we would need them. It would be much more valuable than to have foreign investments than it would be to have the money or capital in our own country. You are able to control your own country anyway, but you cannot tell Uncle Sam or someone else what his nationals are to do. If you have gold or investments in their countries they will be quite willing to take those investments and ship you the necessary goods. I raise this point and perhaps those in charge of the foreign exchange control board will be able to answer me satisfactorily.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of bill No. 193, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I have just a few
remarks to make in amplification of what I said on the introduction of this bill and its first reading.
As hon. members know, the Combines Investigation Act provides for the investigation of trade combinations, monopolies, trusts and mergers which are alleged to have operated to the detriment of the public through limiting production, fixing or enhancing prices, preventing competition or otherwise restraining trade. Organizations of this kind which are against the interest of the public are defined by the act as combines, and participation or knowing assistance in the formation or operation of such combines is an indictable offence.
In outlining the purpose of the amendment on the first reading of the bill on June 5, reference was made to the report "Canada and International Cartels", which was tabled in the house at the last session, and which reported the results of an inquiry into the nature and effects of international cartels and other types of trade combinations. In that report it was submitted that need existed for strengthening the Combines Investigation Act "in certain matters of procedure including the avoidance of unnecessary impediments or delays in the conduct of proceedings under the act", and for "more adequate provision for the initiation of inquiries by the combines investigation commission into restraints of trade and unfair trade practices." The amendments now proposed are designed for that purpose. They do not alter the definition of the offences against which the act provides. The proposed amendments deal with certain matters of procedure for the investigation and prosecution of offences, which are at present defined of collusive, monopolistic and other unfair trade practices which unduly restrain or injure trade. The purpose of the amendments is to provide improvements in the procedure now made available for dealing with trade offences of this class, with a view to facilitating deterrent action respecting the commission of these offences.
The principal changes proposed by the bill are to be found in sections 2 to 6 and section 9. Perhaps I might make a brief reference to these sections, as it is what they contain that determines the nature and extent of the bill.
Combines Investigation

Section 2 provides for the appointment of deputy commissioners who may exercise the powers of the commissioner, subject to control by regulations made by governor in council. It is felt that if the act is to be effectively administered the commissioner cannot possibly conduct all the inquiries which should be made, and the appointment of deputy commissioners would enable them to act in his stead and carry out some duties which the pressure of business might make it impossible for him to attend to personally. It is not intended to provide that the governor in council shall appoint these deputy commissioners; they are to be appointed under the civil service commission, but one of them can be designated by the governor in council after appointment by the civil service commission to perform the duties of the commissioner in his absence or inability to act.
Section 3 authorizes the commissioner to make studies of cartels or other monopolistic conditions, and to report the results to the minister. It is felt that it is apt to be necessary after the abolition of the wartime controls to have studies made of the operations of these large trade organizations so as to prevent if possible, rather than to punish after the fact, conduct of organizations which might be injurious to trade. The impression is that business men in general do not want to be lawbreakers, and if these conditions are inquired into and representations are made to them as to the likelihood of their being in breach of public laws they will most often desist and modify their proceedings in such way as not to fall foul of these provisions of the law.
Section 4 would permit the commissioner to investigate complaints which may indicate breaches of sections 498 and 498 (a) of the criminal code. The several kinds of offences against which the Combines Investigation Act and these two sections of the criminal code provide are very closely related. It will be remembered that in 1935 the dominion trade and industry commission was given jurisdiction to make inquiries under the Combines Investigation Act and also into suspected breaches of these two sections of the criminal code. Then, after the hearing before the courts in 1937, the jurisdiction over the application of the combines act was removed from the dominion trade and industry commission, but it was left with jurisdiction to make inquiries into breaches of sections 498 and 198 (a>
of the criminal code, frequently into the same matters which might be handled under the Combines Investigation Act. It is felt that it will be more convenient and avoid

duplication to have investigations under control of one agency, whether nominally they be under the Combines Investigation Act or under sections 498 and 498 (a) of the criminal code. The chairman of the dominion trade and industry commission warmly approves the transfer of this jurisdiction to investigate under the articles of the code to the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act, and his recommendation is concurred in by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), under whose jurisdiction the dominion trade and industry commission operates.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
Will the minister permit a question with regard to the new section 10A?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am coming to that.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
But it is section 4 of the act. Since the purpose of these amendments is to have machinery which will operate quickly and more effectively than that previously in operation, why is it provided that only the attorney-general of Canada or the attorney-general of the province within which an offence is alleged to have taken place has the right to institute proceedings? W'hy, if enforcement of this act is desired, should not any group of persons have the right to lay an information under the act?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: It is my impression, Mr. Speaker, that anyone would have the right to lay complaints, but here, if an information is to be laid as the result of an investigation conducted by the commissioner, it is felt that that should be on the responsibility of the attorney-general of a province or the attorney-general of Canada. My hon. friend knows what prejudices may sometimes exist about certain practices which appear to be monopolistic. We had an illustration of that in the investigation of the royal commission on coal policy. At more places than one people went before the commission and attempted to make out that there existed monopolies operating in the coal trade to the detriment of the public. There had been a few years ago an investigation by the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act; at that time it was found that there were practices which were contrary to the policy of the code and of the Combines Investigation Act, and proceedings were instituted on behalf of the attorney-general of the province of Quebec. They constituted quite a considerable undertaking. I know something about it, because I was retained by the attorney-general of Quebec to prosecute, and a very large bill was incurred in the prosecution of those offences. Whenever there is an

Combines Investigation
investigation and there are revealed things which are detrimental to the public, it has been the policy, since the act was first introduced, in 1910, to make it the responsibility of the attorney-general of the province concerned or the attorney-general of Canada to institute the proceedings and to finance them to a judgment. A charge could be laid by anyone on his own information, on his own belief, under section 498 or 498(a) of the criminal code, if one saw fit to do so. However, for the purposes of setting in motion the action of the courts as a consequence of investigations made by the commissioner it was felt that it would be desirable to have the matter under the control of one of the attorneys-general representing the whole public.
Section 5 authorizes the commissioner in certain circumstances to initiate inquiries, and thus restores a provision to the same effect which had been in the section from 1923 to 1937. It is felt that as government wartime controls are removed there will be increasing need to avoid unnecessary delays in seeking the facts as to any private restrictive agreements that might prevent or unduly limit the supply of goods or enhance their prices unreasonably. Most of these inquiries are not extensive and are intended to be rather preventive and advisory in character, and it is the view that administration rvill be more effective if the power to initiate such inquiries, without the necessity of producing a complaint by six persons, is restored.
In section 6 of the bill, the first proposed subsection 2A is to consolidate and revise a restriction placed in the act in 1937. It restricts the power to enforce orders on witnesses to attend and testify, which is an ordinary and needed formal power of a commissioner conducting investigations under any statute or commission. The mere existence of this power is usually sufficient; it has been used only once under the act since 1923, and may never have to be used again, because, when it exists, one does not usually attempt to resist and require that enforcement proceedings be taken.
Here the restrictions left in this provision of the bill are quite substantial. They are not found in any other statute. It was felt, however, that in view of their insertion in 1937, after a commissioner sentenced for contempt one who happened to be a lawyer, they should be retained in substance, and it may be a good safeguard to have to apply to a judge before resort to these enforcement provisions, which are usually in all other statutes authorizing inquiries.
Subsection 2A of section 6 is intended to replace section 42 of the act as it now exists. Subsection 2B would authorize a justice, on application of the commissioner, to transfer to the commissioner things that are seized pursuant to a search warrant issued by a justice under the provisions of the criminal code. It may be necessary for the commissioner to retain for the purposes of the prosecution the papers found on execution of the search warrant, and it was felt here again that the matter should not be left to the arbitrary decision of a commissioner but that he should be required to justify before a justice the propriety of retaining the things found in the execution of the search warrant.
Section 9 represents the principal substantive change in the bill. It authorizes the exchequer court to issue an order revising or cancelling patent licensing or pooling agreements or agreements relating to the use of trade marks or patents when these have been used to the detriment of the public. The cartel report showed how patent rights may on occasion be used as pretext and shields for activities which would be clearly illegal under the Combines Investigation Act if patents were not involved. Trade marks may be used as an adjunct to restrictive patent licensing agreements or employed by themselves to enforce arrangements as to the division of markets. This section is designed not to interfere with the proper use of trade marks or patent rights or deprive patentees of rewards for their inventions. It is intended to provide a means for ensuring that trade marks and patents will not be used to control an industry to the detriment of the public at large, and to furnish a workable way of preventing persons from extending patent rights beyond their legitimate bounds by using them as instruments for restrictive cartel arrangements and for the exercise of wider and unreasonable private monopoly controls. A close analogy to the type of exchequer court order proposed already exists in certain sections of the Patent Act which are designed to prevent abuses of patents by way of failure to work the patents in this country. The proposed section has a wider purpose which makes it desirable to place it in this act rather than in the Patent Act.
The general form of procedure and order is not at variance with established court procedure respecting patents. This would allow the exchequer court, instead of making an order cancelling a patent or cancelling the registration of a trade mark, to make a lesser order, if it were felt that a lesser order than absolute cancellation would prevent the undesirable effects of the use being made of the
Combines Investigation

patent or trade mark. Previously, one had to make out a case that appeared sufficiently grave to the court to justify the cancellation of the patent; whereas here, the court will not have to go to that extreme. It may be that it will be sufficient for the court to enjoin a certain form of use of the patent or trade mark.
The principal effect of section 10 is to permit the attorney general of Canada to arrange for prosecution of a combine without in practice having to wait at least three months, as under the existing section, to determine whether the attorney general of a province concerned is going to take action. Under the act as it stands, a report has to be made to the attorney general of a province and the attorney general of Canada has to wait three months to see whether the provincial attorney general will act or m.t before authorizing action himself. There may be cases where it would be found desirable to proceed without waiting for that length of time for a decision from the provincial attorney general. There may be such things as extend to more than one province, where it might not be right to expect that the attorney general of one province would undertake the prosecution of all those concerned in a widespread combine or restrictive arrangement. In the past the prosecution has been taken with the assistance or under the direction of the attorney general of Canada. The provincial departments have usually required the attorney general of Canada to undertake financial responsibility for the proceedings. Some of the recommendations of the report are being carried out as a result of the supply voted to the department for the combines investigation branch; and there have already been organizational changes designed to implement parts of the report of the commission. It is felt that if the house sees fit to make these amendments to the statute, we shall then have a fairly effective instrument to carry out the objectives indicated in this cartel report, which, after it was tabled in the house at the last session, obtained wide publicity and, I believe, fairly wide approval throughout the country. It is felt that there is now a responsibility upon the commission to put itself in shape to do those things which it recommended and which seem to have met with pretty general approval throughout the country.

speechtext:
In my view this is an important measure. The principal act, of course, is itself most important and in principle it has my most thorough approval. I support the original act and this amendment on the ground that it is one of our most effective safeguards

against socialism. Even those who are as enthusiastic supporters of the free enterprise system as I am will not deny that under free enterprise, as under any economic order, we have weaknesses. I believe that the Combines Investigation Act is one practical means of ensuring that free enterprise shall continue to be the enterprise of liberty and not of licence. Over one hundred years ago Edmund Burke said, "Liberty must be limited in order to be possessed." I hasten to add now that in my view the only proper limitation to liberty is a limitation imposed by parliament and not by any other agency, but perhaps that is by the way. It is this direct form of limitation, this direct action against particular weaknesses of our economic system, which will best purge free enterprise of what I call its Achilles heel, and will at the same time save us from the burdens, repressions and restrictions-and in particular from the danger to political liberty-which are always inherent in any general form of regulation such as socialism.
The weakness of the free enterprise system has always been that it has failed to solve completely the problems of equitable distribution of wealth. One of these problems, and not its least, is the control of combinations and monopolies which act against the public interest. The fact that these problems have not been solved before is not, I believe, due to any evil which exists in the Canadian people but rather because of the great difficulty of devising proper measures for their control. Therefore to say that because these problems exist and have not yet been completely solved we should embrace socialism is to step from the frying-pan into the fire; because apart from its most important threat to political liberty, without which no economic benefits would be of much use, nor would they be lasting, it is my view that socialism would aggravate rather than assuage the problems which confront us with respect to the distribution of wealth. Although under free enterprise the distribution of wealth may be imperfect, the fact remains that under that same system we have been able to create a system of production which has never been equalled by any other economic order and which, I believe, can never be so equalled. That ability to produce wealth to maximum quantity under free enterprise is, perhaps, the reason which makes it possible to bear our present admittedly defective system of distribution.
It is interesting to reflect that in fact we are living under socialism now and that we have, as we might expect, underproduction and an unwieldy and bureaucratic system' of

Combines Investigation
distribution. Under any other form of socialism practised by any other party I feel sure that we would have the same unwieldy and bureaucratic system of distribution which would be worse than the difficulties which I have admitted to exist under the free enterprise system.
It is interesting to note that in the last report of the Department of Labour for the year ended March 31, 1945, it is stated that this monopolistic danger which is inherent in all controls may be enhanced by the wartime prices and trade board. No less an authority than the chairman of the board is quoted in these words in the report to which I refer:
In some cases the continuance of such controls beyond the emergency would have the effect of restricting competition and production, and of strengthening the position of established busi-nesess. I think you will agree that this would be most undesirable. To create a healthy and prosperous economy more competition and more freedom for newcomers to start up in business is needed-not less. That is one of the principal reasons why such controls have to be eliminated as soon as feasible and before the emergency is quite gone rather than after.
I may say that during the past few months I had occasion to investigate and to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) one small case in which the principle referred to by the chairman of the board was, in my opinion, in fact operating to damage the small businessman in relation to his greater competitors. Therefore I believe this act goes in the right direction.
At this time I wish to say that in the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act we have a public servant who is performing a great service to the country. One has only to meet him to recognize two things about him: first, that he realizes the importance and the far-reaching effect that his job has if it is properly done; and, second, that he also recognizes what a delicate position he is in and how carefully he must guide himself in carrying out the provisions of the act without becoming a burden upon or an irritant to the business community. I believe that Mr. McGregor has a clear realization of those essential principles.
I believe that the day is surely going to come in this country when business relationships and practices such as we are dealing with here, as well as industrial relationships, labour-management relations, will be regulated by as clear a code of laws as now govern the personal relationship between man and man. Time was when such things as slavery, duelling, child labour and many less obvious malpractices between human beings were supported by law and were considered to be
perfectly proper things. That time, of course, is no more. Likewise it is my belief that the time will come when all of us will recognize the evils to self and to society generally which are inherent in many trade practices which at the present time are considered, and widely considered, to be perfectly proper means of doing business. When that time comes; when we all have that realization, I am quite certain these malpractices which are themselves partly the cause of our inequitable distribution of wealth, will disappear. I feel we must all work toward that end, but in the meantime we must resist the temptation to follow the seeming short-cuts but actual blind alleys of socialism. I believe the proper regulator of ordinary business relationships and practices, and of labour-management disputes, is the same authority that now regulates our personal relations as between ourselves; and when I speak of that authority I mean public opinion translated into law, not actions of the executive government.
Before I turn to the actual bill before us, I want to make one observation as to the dangers always inherent in the other form of monopoly, what one might call public monopoly or the commodity agreement. It is very proper that under this act the commissioner does not inquire or investigate into a combination which has received the approval of this house or of any provincial legislature. I wish now simply to observe that the fact that there is no check over monopolistic practices on the part of a public body, through the Combines Investigation Act or in any other way, places upon this house and upon provincial legislatures an added responsibility to make sure that in bringing about any such combination, or in giving it their approval, for a seemingly good purpose they are not running counter to the principle expressed in this bill.
Turning to the bill itself, I want to say that I believe it really does not go far enough. Section 30, which is the only substantial alteration of the law in the bill, is very good as far as it goes, but it is entirely adjective law. It is a strengthening of the procedure and penalties laid down for the punishment and check of breaches of the law; but I see in the bill no new departure in substantive law, no development of the law in the light of our experience in business over the twenty or thirty years since the Combines Investigation Act was first enacted. It is my view, following definitely along what I said in principle, that together with its enforcement duties an equal function of this department should be the development of what one might call the legal science respecting combinations and business
Combines Investigation

practices. In other words, this department should be an educational agency as well as an enforcement agency; and out of this department should come the new substantive law which will enable'our business men to regulate their practices with greater certainty and less chance of having their ordinary business interfered with by investigation or executive action. I realize that the problem of developing new and substantive law in this connection is very great. It- is difficult to isolate what are bad business practices from those that are tolerable; and it is my suggestion to the minister that an attempt might be made around the fringes of this whole subject so that the malpractices which we know to exist but which we cannot translate accurately into law may be confined and narrowed by the isolation of those which are clearly immoral, if you like to use that term, and which can be prohibited by law. In that connection I want to refer to a footnote at page 209 of Mr. Bladen's "Introduction to Political Economy," where in dealing with this question of the public knowledge of what is or is not evil in business practice he gives three quotations:
See J. Finkelman, "Combines and Public Policy":
"One of the gravest faults of the whole legislation is that owing to the uncertainty and obscurities of the law a person may be accused and convicted of having committed a criminal offence when he was doing no more than what he considered desirable to forward his own interests in the manner generally approved in the industrial society in which he operates. The line between what is legal and what is illegal is very fine, and his guilt or innocence may depend to a large extent on the social and economic views of the registrar, or the commissioner, or the judge and jury. It is highly desirable in the interests of justice that the offender be not punished unless he has been warned that his conduct is unsocial and until he is given an adequate opportunity of reorganizing his enterprise."
Then the author refers to the remarks of L. M. Singer, organizer of the amalgamated builders' council and other guilds, who said:
Every court and every jury may reach a *different decision upon the same facts. Until they speak it is not known whether the accused is a malefactor or a benefactor.
Then he refers to the editorial comment in the Financial Times of August 1, 1941, on the [DOT]conviction of a group of tobacco manufacturers and wholesalers:
The "crime" for which the companies have been convicted is one that has been considered for many years good business and merchandising policy.
In reading these words I do not want it thought that I entirely agree with all the [DOT]conclusions at which those persons arrived. Bather I quote them only to show what is
| Mr. Merritt.]
in fact the case, that there is considerable uncertainty in the minds of many people as to what is or what is not an offence under the law as it stands at present in relation to business practices. That is a justification for the views I have read. On the other hand, one could say what I said to myself after reading that footnote, which was that the only time I had heard this before was in the old adage, "I didn't know it was loaded". That revolver analogy is quite interesting, because the time was when in this and in all countries the possession of a revolver or a firearm in a private home was absolutely necessary for the protection of life. At that time the law was not so developed that the individual householder could feel safe under its protection and he had to provide means of protecting himself. Thus we all had revolvers or other firearms in our homes. However, that day has gone, and now all of us can feel perfectly safe and know that we shall be properly protected by the police without the necessity of our having revolvers in our homes. The result is that now we are harder on people who do not know it was loaded than we were, say one hundred years ago. By the development and strengthening of the law relating to business practices we could then be harder on those who do not know that the industrial revolver is loaded.
We must consider the problem of creating new law and the new public opinion which should precede or accompany that law. We must consider the difficulty of education in this field. I do not think that can be done through the national film board, the newspapers or any other similar agency. I would throw out the suggestion that the best possible educator would be the isolation of malpractices and their prohibition by law. We should have these safeguards as well as the general provisions that are now to be found in the criminal code and the act.
If you examine the history of investigations and prosecutions under the Combines Investigation Act since it was established, I believe in 1910, you cannot avoid being impressed with the number of cases where the commissioner felt that either combinations or improper trade practices existed but where no prosecution followed or where the courts, on prosecution being instituted following the report of the commissioner, acquitted the accused. There, again, we can see difficulties in our substantive law. In my opinion the reason for the acquittal is quite evident. Where the words "unduly or unreasonably to restrict" are found in section 498 or where in the Combines Investigation Act there are found such words as "or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interests of

Combines Investigation
the public, whether consumers, producers or otherwise," there is thrown upon the court, not the duty of determining that a certain fact or agreement exists but rather the duty of determining what we in this parliament so far have been unable to determine, whether the agreement or the facts as found by the court are in the interests or against the interests of the Canadian people. Everyone knows that very descriptive quotation, "Our lady of the common law is no economist." In a few words that is the reason why convictions are not obtained in some cases after the commissioner has found evidence of malpractice.
I have one or two suggestions to make with regard to the need for the development of substantive law, which may show the way in which these forward steps could be taken. Hon. members will recall that in the two investigations into alleged combines in connection with fruit distributors in western Canada the commissioner passed unfavourably upon the existence of control by the jobber or by the distributor over the broker who sells to the jobber and who is actually the agent of the grower. In both investigations the commissioner pointed out the danger of the exercise of that control over the broker by his natural antagonist in business. The broker would be disposed to favour the jobber to the disadvantage of the grower, whose agent he was.
If the commissioner's findings were so in fact, and I believe in the first case they were held to be so by the court upon prosecution, it would seem to me that there is a clear case which could be isolated and which could be enacted into substantive law in order to ensure that the business agent will have a single loyalty and not be controlled by the person to whom he is selling.
Then, again, we have cases of price fixing at the retail level by the wholesaler or by the manufacturer or by associations of wholesalers and manufacturers. It is my view that we should set our face against price fixing in business. I do not like public price fixing in principle, and I certainly like it less in private. Prima- facie a lower price to the consumer brought about by competition is a good thing, and the lower the price can go, the better. If at any time, particularly in times of depression, there is need for collective action to prevent the demoralization of a market, then I suggest that application could be made to parliament by those interested-this application should not be to the government or to a commissioner but to parliament itself-for 63260-193
the institution of a marketing board to regulate prices, preserve the market from demoralization and perhaps to maintain employment.
It is my view that only in depression times would such an application be necessary. In normal times of buoyant business one does not find these combinations arising so much, nor does one find that prices go down to such a level that demoralization sets in. It might be interesting to consider what happened in British Columbia where we had a peculiar situation in pre-depression time in the marketing of fruit. Our markets were far away and they were difficult of access to the grower. There was created a natural products marketing board under provincial legislation to assist that body of our economy which had a clear need. Later on, when the depression set in and all markets were becoming shaky and tending toward demoralization we had a succession of boards set up on the Pacific coast covering milk, potatoes and many other products. Of course we have a great example of price fixing approved by the government with respect to the pulp and paper industry in Quebec and Ontario. It is my view, although I do not pretend to have studied the matter to a finality, that we might well simply make unlawful private price-fixing agreements, and allow those whose markets are so peculiar as to require collective action to go to their respective legislatures or to this parliament for the necessary authority.
In this field of legislation we cannot expect miracles all at once. What I should like to see is steps taken progressively over the years in prohibiting those malpractices which are capable of isolation. As we go along over a period of years I think we would find that such a course would have a beneficial effect on the distribution of the wealth of the countiy.
Great emphasis should be placed by the minister upon the education * of the public through the development of substantive law and also by action of parliament and of the judiciary to check those practices which tend against the public interest. He should particularly avoid the extension of action by the executive, which in my view amounts to regimentation, whereas the action of parliament and of the judiciary amounts to wholesome and progressive regulation.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) will not mind if my first words are words of congratulation upon his progress in social thinking since he came into this house. But I regret that I am not able as yet to congratulate him on the clarity of his thought. He began by saying

Combines Investigation

that he favoured this measure because it was a means of combating or retarding socialism, and then before he had made much further progress with his speech he told the house that we have socialism already. If we have socialism already, obviously the thing to do is not to retard' it but to do everything we can to facilitate its development and make it more and more useful.
I cannot, however, agree with his conclusions because they were negative. He would use the law, the courts and the police to stop the malpractices and the exploitation of the community by corporations which have got control of our means of life and are using it not for the purpose of providing the community with what they need but to make private fortunes for themselves out of the needs of the community. Obviously the remedy is not the appointment of more policemen but to take over the operation of these industries by the people themselves and operate them for the benefit of the people.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext: You mean, by the government.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
The government is a
government of the people and acts on behalf of the people.
I can agree with my hon. friend that this bill does not go far enough. In so far as it goes it is made necessary by the public demand, and the effect which that public demand has on the government, for some form of control over monopolistic corporations.
There is another thing in which I agree most heartily with the member for Vancouver-Burrard, and that is in his remarks with regard to the commissioner. It is my good fortune to have known the commissioner for almost the fifteen years or so that I have been in this house. I have watched his work in his department, and I can agree with the hon. member that he has done a good job in so far as the law would allow him to do it.
Canada is relatively a young industrial country. Within the lifetime of the older members of this house and perhaps of those like myself who are not so old we have seen this country develop from a nation of handicrafts to an industrial nation with huge combinations and monopolies. As far back as 1910 we had our first combines law. Since then, we have had a number of commissions investigate industrial conditions in Canada. Perhaps the most notable of them was the price spreads and mass buying commission, the chairman of which was the Hon. II. H. Stevens, who was the first minister of trade and commerce in the Bennett government. The com-

mission was appointed in 1934. In the introduction to its report made in 1935 the commission says:
At first sight, indeed, it appeared that the separate and distinct problems which emerged in the evidence called for separate treatment and almost separate reports. On closer study, however, it became clear that many of the grievances complained of, and the problems disclosed, were manifestations of one fundamental and far-reaching social change, the concentration of economic power. This idea, therefore, runs through the whole of our report and gives it a certain unity which it might not otherwise possess.
The Combines Investigation Act in the first instance was brought into being because of the power of combines to control and use the means of production in this country, not for the benefit of the people, but for their own profit. There was an amendment to the act in 1935, and the late leader of this group raised the question of giving publicity to the commissioner's reports. My memory is that the government of the day was opposed to doing that; I am not sure whether it was made the law or not. I should like to read a very short statement by the present Minister of Finance (Mr Ilsley), who was a member of the price spreads and mass buying commission. He did not sign the whole report, or at least he signed it with reservations.
He said, as reported in Hansard of 1935, page 3474:	-
I just want to add to what I said that the evidence before the price spreads commission revealed a startling concentration of business in Canada, great numbers of large corporations and what the experts call monopolies and quasimonopolies. Times are changing. It may have been quite proper twenty or thirty years ago to be very careful as to what publicity you gave to matters of this kind, but it is highly important in these latter days that the public have all the facilities possible for coping with these great concentrations of industry, and to that end it seems to me important that the public be acquainted with the true state of affairs.
Then he continued:
This act is being amended not only to cover combines but to give better facilities for coping with monopolies such as mergers and the like, and it is exceedingly important that tile public be acquainted at once on the conclusion of an investigation with the true state of affairs. If for instance 85 per cent of the packing industry gets into the hands of one company, which is what would happen if two of the largest companies were to merge at the present time, that is a fact which the public should know, and know ' at once.
I wanted to read that because it shows how strong monopolies are in this country and what very slight moves are necessary on their part to make them even stronger.
Again, in the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission on dominion-provincial affairs, which was later than the price spreads report, I find this at page 148 of book 1:

Combines Investigation
Business organization has everywhere become increasingly monopolistic. In Canada industry, commerce and finance are highly centralized and in many branches a few enterprises dominate the field. Under such conditions the maintenance of prices is possible in the face of declining demands. The monopolistic producers may consider that they are better off by selling less at higher prices than by selling more at lower prices.
That, of course, has always been the main purpose of a monopoly, a combine or a cartel -to sell less for more. You are not going to eradicate that tendency by the policeman's baton or by the fear of a term in gaol, particularly when corporations have such great financial means at their command to protect them from going to gaol. This report continues:
Consequently, the burden tends to fall upon the workers who lose their jobs through the reduction in output and on the exporters whose costs are thus held rigid while their prices on world markets are sharply reduced.
I am not surprised that, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard studies these things, while he is still bracing himself against socialism, he agrees that we have to do something. To doubt is the beginning of wisdom.
I need not say anything more to show that Canada is the home of many monopolies and perhaps cartels as well. I imagine that hon. members have read the report on "Canada and International Cartels" which was tabled in this house at the last session. This group have been drawing these matters to the attention of parliament in season and out of season ever since we have been here. We continued to do so during the war. Cartels did not decline during the war; they prospered and are stronger than ever they were. At the beginning of 1943 a special parliamentary committee was set up to hear evidence regarding the Aluminum Company of Canada and a special depreciation of S164 million which was given to it by this government in addition to the wartime profits that were made by the company. The committee admitted in the report to the house that an international holding company, located in Switzerland, limited world production of aluminum, fixed world minimum prices, and, further, that the German producer was a member of this holding company. It further pointed out that from 1935 this aluminum, cartel, by agreeing to restrict production to the needs of domestic markets, allowed Germany to expand aluminum production enormously. The cost of that may or perhaps may not be computed in the lives needlessly lost during the recent war. Recently the United States court of appeal ruled that the Aluminum Company of America' and Aluminium Limited of Canada were engaged in cartel agreements. In 63260-193i
addition to this, the cartel's report to which I have referred, a report ordered by the Canadian government, may I point out, states, at page 34:
The aluminum industry throughout the world has been dominated by a small number of firms since it became of commercial importance toward the close of the nineteenth century. The first cartel was formed in 1901 and the latest, and most effective, Alliance Aluminum Company of Basle, was set up under an agreement made in 1931 and renewed in 1936. The present Canadian producer. Aluminium Limited, or its predecessors entered into each cartel. Aluminium Limited was formed in 1928 and received from the Aluminum Company of America practically all its foreign properties in return for common stock, which was then distributed to shareholders of Alcoa. The new Canadian company, Aluminium Limited, became a member of the Alliance Aluminum Company of Basle with a production quota of 28-58 per cent, compared with 21-36 for the French producer, 15-42 for the Swiss, 19-46 for the German and 15 for the British. Aluminum Company of America was not a party to the cartel arrangement, but it seems to have been accepted that Alcoa would not upset the market outside the United States while the cartel arrangement would preclude any competitive sales in the American market.
The control of the world trade in- aluminum was to be achieved by the Alliance through three devices:
(a)	by fixing an Alliance buying price at which it would purchase aluminum from any member producing within its quota;
(b)	by regulating the production quotas of its members, thus protecting, itself against actually having to buy raw aluminum at the price fixed under (a);
(c)	by holding surplus stock off the market (the 1931 agreement provided for the purchase, at a stated price, of surplus stocks in the hands of members).
Then, at page 35, we find this:
In view of the monopolistic character of the aluminum industry in most producing countries and the national interests involved, some positive form of intergovernmental action may be required in this field in the post-war period to avoid undue restriction of production.
I submit that positive action means not merely action through the courts. Then, again, we have C.I.L., that is, Canadian Industries Limited, which is a wholly-owned- subsidiary of du Pont of the United States and Imperial Chemical Industries of the United Kingdom. It was stated in the press a few days ago that the United Kingdom government was making plans to nationalize Imperial Chemical Industries in that country. In 1939 the directors of du Pont passed a resolution permitting this Canadian industry', that is Canadian Industries Limited, to export during the war. If they could permit this Canadian company to export during the war, it -meant that the Canadian company had- not the right to export before the war. Here is a flagrant example of pre-war restrictive policies on- the part of the -mono-
Combines Investigation

polies-a private company in one country deciding what one of its branches in another country shall or shall not do.
I doubt whether there is in the bill before us, when it is passed by this parliament, anything that will prevent that kind of thing. It is stated in the report that international cartels rest upon and arise out of national monopolistic organizations. There must first be a monopoly of a national character and that monopoly extends to the international field.
I quote again from the report:
The restrictive practices^ followed by international cartels are similar in character to those engaged in by domestic trade combinations. In fact, the agreements are in most cases made effective through the actions of domestic combinations or monopolies. '
The report goes on to cite a number of combines, and one of the examples mentioned is that of fertilizers, particularly potash, nitrogen and phosphorus, of which Canada imports about $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 worth annually. That was before the war. Prices were deliberately kept high for this product. Production of the materials was restricted, with the ultimate result that the farmers suffered; and when the farmers of a country suffer, the whole population suffers. Another example given was that of magnesium refractories. However, since all this is in the report I will not take up the time of the house to deal with it. Let me quote briefly from page 55:
To the extent that cartels attempt to resist change and maintain the status quo, to prefer security to progress, they tend to impoverish the world. In the post-war world this will be a particularly undesirable attitude. In the first place, the great technological advances of the war period must be applied to peace-time industries. New competitive products and new sources of supply of old products will emerge. Such new developments must not be throttled at birth hy defenders of the status quo.
If my hon. friends think they are going to prevent that sort of demonstration of power by court action and not by positive action, in the form of creating industries which these people will not build, they will be greatly disappointed.
In the second place, the development of backward countries must take place if the promise of "freedom from want" is intended to apply to more than a small fraction of the world's population . . . Industrialization of undeveloped countries will provide immediately new opportunities for investment and the sale of capital goods, and should assist initially in maintaining a high level of employment in the older industrial countries.
But that will not be possible as long as we are thinking in terms of high prices rather than in terms of quantity of production; and monopolies-indeed all private business- must, because of their very nature, think of prices rather than of quantity and quality.
