speechtext:
May I read another passage from page 66:
The allocation of markets through restrictive arrangements made by private interested parties impinges on government authority over foreign trade and may nullify national trade policies developed to serve wider public markets. Government policies to encourage either imports or exports may prove ineffective if private barriers to such trade are erected by cartels. The reservation of the domestic market to particular producers may be as effective as the prohibitory tariff in barring imports. The allocation of import or export quotas by cartel agreement subjects foreign trade to quantitative limitation, though such control may run counter to public policy. Ways must be found to prevent private business organized as cartels from supplanting government in the establishment of such commercial policies.
I submit that there is nothing in the Combines Investigation Act and nothing in the amendment before us that provides ways of preventing private business organized as cartels from supplanting governments in the establishment of commercial policies.
Then again:
Cartel arrangements which impede industrial innovations and slow down the effective development of new opportunities for investment tend to diminish the supply of goods available for human use. Attempts by cartels to protect old investments by limiting the introduction of use-

Combines Investigation
ful new techniques and new production would have a prejudicial effect on government policies to secure high employment.
At a time when, the purpose of this government, as stated by them almost every day, is to secure high employment, the first thing that they should do-and they may not succeed even in that-is to make sure that their policies are not impeded by the control over the resources of the country, both industrial and natural, by a few individuals or corporations.
I shall give another quotation from page 68, which reads as follows:
The following might be considered in the further development and application of Canadian policy relating to both domestic and international practices in restraint of trade:
(a) The full utilization of Canadian legislative powers with respect to criminal law,-
That is what the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard is advocating.
-including investigations, publicity and prosecution under the Combines Investigation Act, tariffs, import and export trade, _ taxation, patents, trade marks, public ownership, including crown companies and the disposal of war assets, and public regulation, in so far as such powers may be constitutionally applied.
This report was not made by a C.C.F. commission, but by a commission of experts appointed by the government. They had full information on what was happening to the Canadian economy and to world-wide economy. According to this statement, they were convinced that legislation in itself, so long as it is confined to investigation and prosecution, is not sufficient to meet the situation. What has happened in Canada is happening in every industrial country in the world.
In May, 1944, Wendel Berge, then attorney general of the United States said:
Make no mistake-the war has not interfered with cartel plans. Cartel agreements invariably provide for the contingency of war. Long before the war, cartels worked out a modus vivendi-a method of continued existence-for they felt that their relations must be preserved, war or no war. Thus we find American and British cartelists agreeing to preserve the German position in Latin American markets after the war. Agreements between the cartel members of the countries now at war provide for a resumption at the war's close.
I think I have said-and I merely quoted from publications which are available to every hon. member-sufficient to prove to us that it is desirable not only that we pass this legislation but that we give every facility to the commission or commissioners who may be appointed to carry on the work which they have done so well during the years, having regard to the limitations imposed upon them. We must also take more positive steps if we are to make the natural and industrial
resources of this country available to the people so that wealth production will be limited only by our willingness to work.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
I wish to commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and those associated with him for having introduced these amendments to the Combines Investigation Act. I think they will serve the public interest and they are, therefore, a step in the right direction. Without any hesitation I should like to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) when he referred to the splendid work done by commissioner F. A. McGregor. I often think that few people in Canada are aware of their great indebtedness to that official.
In speaking on this topic this afternoon let me say at once that, generally speaking, I have no quarrel with combines or cartels as such. It is only when certain combines conflict with the public interest, when for selfish purposes they attempt to restrain trade, when by so-called "gentlemen's agreements" or otherwise, they endeavour to eliminate competition, thereby to gain monopolistic privileges; it is when that sort of thing is attempted that I am prepared, as I believe thousands of other Canadians are, to fight to the limit any such cartels, no matter what label they bear.
I am particularly interested in the attitude of what appears to be two such combines operating in Canada at the present time, but I shall discuss only one of them to-day. I may return to the other at a later date. Here I want to emphasize the fact that I do not for a moment believe that all combines are operating on purely selfish principles. Far from it; on the contrary, I believe that combines or unions among business or manufacturing firms often result in lower operating expenses than might otherwise be possible. If a reasonable percentage of the reduction is passed on to consumers without any restraint of trade or where there is no suggestion of monopolistic practices, the existence of a cartel may be amply justified. At the same time the individual retailer, to whom some reference has been made by the last speaker and some others, operating on his own, in a centre large or small, should not be forgotten, and it must be kept in mind that other factors frequently enter into the community picture, more important perhaps than a trifling difference in the cost of commodities. No one will deny that many a retailer, because of his initiative, his business ability, his fine public spirit, is of untold value in his community.
I do not wish to take up time in generalities, but I want to make special, and I trust, fair reference to the cartel which I have
Combines Investigation

in mind. In view of a situation existing in the western provinces, which would seem to be completely unjustifiable, and desiring to have correct information at the proper time, I placed upon the order paper on March 28, 1946, a number of questions which were duly answered as follows:
1.	Where are the head offices of Canadian Industries Limited, located?
Answer: (from the Secretary of State Department)
Letters patent incorporating Canadian Explosives, Limited, dated 18th November, 1910, provided for the head office of the company to be at the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec. By supplementary letters patent dated 20th June, 1927, the corporate name was changed from Canadian Explosives Limited to Canadian Industries Limited. The annual summary of the company filed under the provisions of section 121 of the Companies Act, as at the 31st March, 1945, recites its street address as 1135 Beaver Hall Hill. Montreal, Quebec.
2.	Is this company associated with any nonCanadian companies that are members of an international cartel? If so, what companies and what cartels?
Answer (from Department of Justice)
Canadian Industries Limited has been associated with Imperial Chemical Industries, Limited, of Great Britain, and E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company of the United States in the general field of chemicals and chemical products. Canadian Industries Limited had agreement with other non-Canadian companies respecting patents or manufacturing rights including an agreement with National Lead Company of the United States with respect to titanium compounds.
Then questions 3 and 4:
Are any of the products of Canadian Industries Limited protected by Canadian tariffs? Is the manufacture of small arms ammunition so protected? If so, at what rate?
The answer from the Department of National Revenue was:
The rates of duty on small arms ammunition
are as follows:
British preferential tariff....10	per	centIntermediate tariff	27i	per	centGeneral tariff	30	per	cent
When the product or manufacture of Great Britain and imported direct to Canada, there is a discount of 50 per cent from the British preferential tariff, or 5 per cent net.
Then question 5:
What has been the total amount of small arms ammunition imported into Canada each year from 1943 to date?
The answer by the Department of Trade and Commerce was:
With reference to part 5 of the question by Mr. Matthew's (Brandon), notice of which appeared in Foies and Proceedings No. 2, part 1, the dominion bureau of statistics do not classify small arms ammunition separately for statistical purposes.
Those were the questions I asked, Mr. Speaker, and that is the information I received from different government departments.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the second reading of bill No. 193, to amend the Combines Investigation Act.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the house rising at six o'clock I was citing some questions which I had placed on the order paper last March and the answers given to them. My reason for having asked those questions, bearing directly as they did upon Canadian Industries Limited, was due to a situation which is set forth and explained by Merchants Consolidated Limited, an old and reputable wholesale firm in the city of Winnipeg of which some four hundred retail merchants in western Canada are members. As hon. members know, I am not in the habit of trespassing unduly upon the time of this house; but because of the number of people interested in this matter, and particularly because of the principle involved, I desire to take the time to place upon the record a brief, issued by Merchants Consolidated Limited so that the Canadian public may judge for themselves the strength or weakness of the situation. I do this not necessarily in the interests of Merchants Consolidated Limited but because, as I have suggested, there is a principle which should be ventilated in discussing the bill now before the house. Here then is the position of Merchants Consolidated Limited as set forth in a letter from them dated November 7, 1945. This letter tells an interesting story, and is as follows:	[DOT]
To our shareholder merchants:
As instructed by the board of directors and the shareholders of Merchants Consolidated Limited, we are writing to advise you of the situation that we face in regard to our ammunition supplies.
In 1914, a number of the better type oi general store and hardware merchants of Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan, noting the inroads being made into retail distribution by the corporate chain-mail-order houses, and
realizing that this type of distribution was detrimental to the community centres of the prairies, met together to discuss the possible establishment of their own wholesale house, with the object in view of establishing economies in the operation that -would result in a more favourable scale of prices to the consuming public and a continuation of prosperous community centres on the prairies.
Merchants Consolidated Limited was organized a few weeks later. A wholesale house was established in Winnipeg and a stock of groceries, dry goods, shoes and hardware merchandise accumulated.
Opposition to a company of this type was early in evidence, and for some years a substantial percentage of the time of the company's management and buyers was devoted to an endeavour to gain for the company recognition as legitimate wholesalers by Canadian, British and American manufacturers.
This was accomplished early in the 1920's in both the grocery and shoe divisions of the company's business, and, with one notable exception, also in the dry goods field.
Recognition, however, was not gained nearly as rapidly in the hardware branch of the company's activities, but, nevertheless, substantial progress was made.
Prior to the war, the company was forced, in order to supply a full range of hardware items to its merchants, to purchase a limited number of lines in the United States of America, although these lines were made in Canada, but were denied to the company by the Canadian manufacturers of them.
The declaration of war, and the institution of a very high rate of exchange for United States currency, and the adoption of a ten per cent war tax. raised the company's costs on these commodities. However, in spite of this, and in spite of the war needs of the United States government, the company was reasonably successful in supplying its merchants with these lines of merchandise.
A number of years ago, the company endeavoured to purchase its ammunition on the same basis as other western wholesale hardware houses from the one and only company making this type of merchandise in Canada-Canadian Industries Limited, with head office in Montreal. The company's management was unsuccessful in persuading this organization to recognize the company as legitimate wholesale buvers at that time.
In order to obtain supplies from a service standpoint, the company was forced to buy from a competitor, at. of course, substantially higher costs than those enjoyed by the company's competitors engaged in a similar line of business.
From time to time, representation was made to Canadian Industries Limited, without satisfactory results.
Shortly after the commencement of the war, it was pointed out to the company that one of the reasons that the company had failed to gain recognition as legitimate hardware wholesalers, with every Canadian manufacturer, was because of the general nature of the company's business. It was suggested that if the company segregated the hardware division from the general business, the company's few purchasing problems would be solved.
Early in 1944. the company obtained a charter for. and established Falcon Hardware Limited, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Merchants Consolidated Limited, and purchased a large building close to the company's premises, and established therein the new company.
Combines Investigation

In the fall of 1944, after this had been accomplished, the management of the company called upon the official in charge of the explosive division of Canadian Industries Limited, at the head office of the company in Montreal, and informed him of the company's action, and once again requested recognition as legitimate wholesalers.
During the course of the discussion, the Canadian Industries Limited official pointed out that ammunition was not denied to the company, as the company had made arrangements to purchase its supplies through a competitor. Your management pointed out that the company was penalized by the amount of profit taken by the competitor on the company's business and that the company, as a legitimate wholesaler, was entitled to buy on a direct basis.
It was further pointed out by the Canadian Industries Limited official that shareholder customers of the company could purchase ammunition from the other wholesalers of the west. The management pointed out, in reply, that over 400 of the leading retail merchants of the prairies had invested substantially in a wholesale company for the privilege of purchasing their goods through that company, and they desired to enjoy this privilege in any and every line of merchandise.
A further meeting with this and other officials of the company was set for the following day, but due to the sudden passing of one of the joint general managers of our company, it was necessary for the engagement to be cancelled.
Early this spring (1945) the management once again called upon the official in charge of the explosive division of Canadian Industries Limited, and after discussing the matter for over two hours failed to obtain a satisfactory reply, and also failed to obtain a satisfactory reason for the manufacturer's attitude.
Your management pointed out to this official that there are in the city of Winnipeg five wholesale hardware houses, including Falcon Hardware Limited, that the other four are on the direct list for ammunition and that he was at a loss to understand why the boycott against the company was persisted in.
Canadian Industries Limited were well aware of the company's purchases through the competitor, and under date of September 11, in reply to a telegram from the company, requesting that they transfer the company's allotment of ammunition to a direct charge to Falcon Hardware Limited stated-"in view of many factors involved in your proposal we would like to postpone a reply regarding 1946 policy until mid-October when we look forward to full discussion with you in Winnipeg."
Early in October, two officials of the explosive division of Canadian Industries Limited called upon the management of the company at Winnipeg and after a lengthy discussion, the company was informed that no change whatever would be made in the policy of the explosive division of Canadian Industries Limited towards Falcon Hardware Limited, although no sound reason for such action was advanced and that Canadian Industries Limited would not sell ammunition to Falcon Hardware Limited.
Canadian Industries Limited enjoy a customs tariff protection on ammunition against manufacturers in the United States of America of 274 per cent and, of course, in addition, the benefit of 104 per cent exchange. This very substantial protection makes it impossible for Falcon Hardware Limited to import into Canada ammunition at competitive prices.

On the high power shotgun shell, made by an American manufacturer in Minnesota, which is comparable in quality to the Imperial shell made by Canadian Industries Limited, the price f.o.b. Minneapolis, less trade discounts, is $31.70 per thousand. The exchange of 104 per cent amounts to $3.33, the import duty of 274 Pet cent is $9.63, the sales tax of 8 per cent is $3.57 and freight $1.10, making a laid down Winnipeg cost ot $49.33 per thousand.
It is the company's understanding that the cost of imperial shells laid down to wholesalers in Winnipeg, who are on the direct list, from Canadian Industries Limited, is $41.87 per thousand.
According to a suggested price list governing selling prices of Manitoba wholesalers to retailers, effective January 2, 1941, and still in effect, imperial 12 ga. shells are listed at $53 per thousand. This represents a mark-up of 26-53 per cent as profit to the wholesaler.
It is obvious from the above-mentioned facts that the company is being discriminated against by the explosive division of Canadian Industries Limited and for which no satisfactory explanation has been advanced. It can further be pointed out that all other divisions of Canadian Industries Limited recognize the company as regular wholesale buyers and extend to the company all terms, discounts, et cetera applying to legitimate wholesalers.
It is the considered opinion of the board of directors of the company that Canadian Industries Limited should either desist from the present discrimination and boycott, and sell its ammunition to Falcon Hardware Limited on the same basis as they sell to all other wholesalers or that the customs tariff on ammunition should be reduced immediately from 274 per cent to 74 per cent, to enable Falcon Hardware Limited and any other Canadian buyer who is being treated in a similar way, to lay ammunition into Canada at prices no higher than those charged by Canadian Industries Limited.
Further, it is the opinion of the company's board that no manufacturer in Canada, enjoying tariff protection, should be permitted now, or at any time in the future, to withhold goods from any legitimate distributor, particularly if the manufacturer enjoys a complete monopoly in his field as does Canadian Industries Limited on ammunition.
Yours very truly.
Merchants Consolidated Limited. November 7, 1945.
If that brief by Merchants Consolidated Limited, a firm that has done business in this country for thirty-two years, does not impute restraint of trade and discriminatory practices, I do not know what does. Surely Canadian Industries Limited have an explanation. Well, they have what purports to 'be an explanation, and here is what they say: I quote from the submission they made under date of January 26, 1946:
The two main objectives of our distribution policy on sporting ammunition have been
1.	To obtain the widest possible retail distribution of our product through hardware and sporting goods outlets.
2.	To supply the largest possible share of Canada's relatively small ammunition market, as maximum volume is necessary for low cost production and maintenance of employment in our

Combines Investigation
factory at Brownsburg, Quebec, where 350 employees are normally engaged solely in the manufacture of sporting ammunition.
I suggest that those two objectives when you analyse them may be reduced to one simple sentence, namely this:	"We want to
obtain the widest possible retail distribution of our product." Well, no one could very well condemn that ambition on the part of any firm. I suggest that in the stand I am taking to-night I am trying to assist C.I.L. in a wider distribution of their product rather than to curtail them. But if C.I.L. are really yearning for expansion as they would suggest, why do they refuse to sell, except at a higher price level, to the wholesale firm of Falcon Hardware company of Winnipeg, which in turn would be distributing to approximately 400 business firms in the western provinces who are stockholders of the Falcon, and whose thousands and thousands of customers are at present deprived by C.I.L. of advantages enjoyed by other Canadian citizens? It would look to me as though C.I.L. is missing a substantial channel for increased distribution, and I can only guess, but I think it is a fairly good guess, as to the reason.
Later in their submission, C.I.L. point out that in keeping with their policy of adequate distribution, a worthy policy I admit, they now sell to eighty wholesalers, who in turn supply 7,000 retail outlets. Well, if their professed policy of adequate distribution is to be genuinely and sincerely adhered to, does it not seem passing strange that C.I.L. in their yearning for expansion are, as I have said, unwilling to increase their wholesalers from eighty even to eighty-one, their retailers from 7,000 to 7,400 or more, and their customers by many thousands? I must say that I have never in all my life seen what seems to me to be a more glaring or a more stupid contradiction in two attitudes as expressed by any firm. I confess that I have tried, but tried in vain, to reconcile those two attitudes, but always with the one result, that is to recall those ancient words, "consistency, thou art a jewel." In theory, anxious to sell, so they say, but in practice refusing to sell except under discrimination. The Canadian public cannot accept any such clumsy explanation as that.
But then the C.I.L. bring up another point which perhaps from their angle would have been more wisely left unsaid:
The choice of distributors is, at best, a difficult one for any manufacturer, particularly when the manufacturer finds himself the sole Canadian producer in competition with numerous imported brands. Our position in this respect has not been created by any combination of interests, but presumably exists because the market is too small (normally less than 1,000,000 per annum 63260-194
divided over 200 types and loads of ammunition) to justify two plants for a product that requires a very large capital investment.
I should like to ask, is this a dog-in-the-manger attitude, or is it not? Does it mean that C.I.L. object to make any outlay for increasing their limited output but yet expect to retain what may be regarded as a monopoly in what they do produce? Are we to infer from their observation that C.I.L. have reached their maximum production? Such a condition would hardly coincide with their urge for adequate distribution. And the last paragraph of their submission seems to be only another contradiction. Here it is:
In order to reach a settlement with Merchants Consolidated Limited we are prepared to submit a proposition for selling them direct on terms which we feel would be fair and reasonable, although ammunition is still in short supply, and we are not able to take care fully of the current needs of our present distributors. We are now attempting to arrange a meeting with Merchants' Consolidated Limited to discuss our proposition . . .
This submission was made by C.I.L. on January 26, 1946. Resulting from it, another letter, dated May 5, was sent by Merchants Consolidated Limited to their members, as follows:
To our shareholder merchants:
Further to our letter to you of November 7, 1945, regarding the refusal of Canadian Industries Limited to recognize Falcon Hardware Limited as legitimate wholesale buyers of ammunition.
On January 26. we received a letter from the sales manager of the "Dominion" ammunition division of Canadian Industries Limited in which he stated that his company was now in a position to discuss the matter with us.
Later, this official wrote to state that he would call upon us either on the following Thursday or Friday. On Friday, February 8 he and his assistant called upon us and presented a letter addressed to this company under date of February 4, in which Canadian Industries Limited agreed to sell to the company on the basis of their "A" list, copy of which they attached to their letter. They stated that this list would be subject to a discount of 2J per cent on carload orders. They also set forth the quantity of ammunition they would be in a position to supply to us in the year 1946.
The prices on the "A" list are 5 per cent higher than the regular list applying to wholesale buyers. In other words we are expected to pay 5 per cent more for ammunition than our competitors.
In view of the fact that the executive committee of our board of directors was to meet on the Monday following the interview, it was decided to leave the matter in abeyance until that meeting.
A report was made to this meeting and, in view of the fact that a general meeting of shareholders of the company had been called for Wednesday, February 13. the executive committee decided that the matter should be taken up at that time with the shareholders.

Combines Investigation

The matter was duly reported to the shareholders and, after some discussion, it was the unanimous opinion that it would be entirely too dangerous for the company to establish a precedent that in effect was that the company was prepared to pay 5 per cent more for its goods than its competitors, and the company was instructed to endeavour through every means possible, to obtain what they originally requested, viz., that the company either be placed on the regular wholesale list by Canadian Industries Limited, or that the rate of customs duty be reduced from 27J per cent to 74 per cent.
Yours very truly,
Merchants Consolidated Limited.
It will be noted from what I have quoted that Merchants Consolidated Limited did not ask for the segregation of their hardware branch under the name of Falcon Hardware Limited, or any other name. The segregation was suggested to them, as stated in their brief.
I suggest that Merchants Consolidated Limited is either a wholesale organization, or it is not. There is no halfway station. I am acquainted with many of the shareholders, and they are the type of men who know their rights, who ask no more, and whose rights they will maintain.
Merchants Consolidated Limited, as hon. members have heard, have been doing a wholesale business in western Canada for thirty-two years. Access to other manufactured products has already been accorded them-dry goods, boots and shoes, groceries, small wares, and many others. Therefore I ask, who is this C.I.L. in Canada, who is this cartel outside Canada having the audacity to set up its own standard of discrimination in this our free country? I know who the members of Merchants Consolidated are and I stand firmly in a demand for justice in their behalf.
This attitude of C.I.L. is not altogether a new thing in Canada. I have some recollection of a similar incident some years ago when another firm enjoying tariff protection declined to sell their products to a wholesale house. I believe that the matter came before the then tariff board and the manufacturers were given their choice of selling the goods as requested, or of having the tariff removed. I need scarcely add that a decision was quickly arrived at. I speak for a multitude of people in this country when I say that C.I.L. should be given the same choice, to be acted upon immediately, namely, to sell to Falcon Hardware in the same way and at the same price as they sell to other hardware firms, or to have the duty removed from similar goods imported into this country. In other words, they should be told to play the game or forfeit their protection. To my mind there is no alterna-

tive. Let it not be forgotten that the Canadian people as a whole, not any one section of them, grant protection to C.I.L. Therefore I say most emphatically that the Canadian people as a whole are entitled to share in the advantages, if any, which accrue from that protection. I would be most reluctant to make demands upon any firm struggling for its existence; but I learn, in fact I have learned to-day, that the common stock of C.I.L. is selling for from S240 to S250 for a $100 share and that a half yearly dividend of three per cent has already been declared for the first half of 1946. It would look, therefore, as if the people of Canada have been reasonably good to C.I.L. and that that firm is not by any means headed for bankruptcy.
I am less fortunate than a good many hon. members in the fact that I am not learned in the law. But I am to some extent learned along certain other lines, perhaps equally as good in their way as that of law. By long and sympathetic observation and by close and friendly contact with my fellow men I have learned something of those principles which are right and just, honourable and desirable in a community and in a nation; and I find it difficult to include in that category any tendency toward discrimination among our people, or the restraint of legitimate trade.
I therefore, with every confidence, ask urgently the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), both able lawyers, to take such steps, either individually or jointly, by the present amendment or by added amendments, as may completely eliminate those unfair conditions to which I strenuously object, and to which I shall continue to object until t'he situation is corrected.
Mr. DAVID A. CROLL (Spadina): I too want to commend Mr. McGregor, who was the commissioner appointed under the Combines Investigation Act, for the comprehensive report which was tabled here last session. The suggestions made in the report as to control and abolishment of cartels are most useful, and I think it is well that before we get into the discussion I should give the house some of the recommendations made by the McGregor commission. A summary states that the cartels were guilty of having:
1.	Limited production and impeded the most efficient use of world resources.
2.	Raised or maintained certain consumer prices.
3.	Restricted the import and export of certain commodities.	_
4.	Restricted the use to which certain commodities might be put.
5.	Nullified external trade policies in certain
respects.	[DOT]

Combines Investigation
6.	Restricted technological advances in certain fields.
7.	Created patent pools or monopolies covering wide fields of endeavour.
8.	Assisted the formation of private industrial empires which tended to supplant governments in the determination of certain national commercial policies.
I think it is fair to say that it is common knowledge that cartels exist, but how they operate is far less familiar, and what is often lost sight of is their effect upon the national economy of this country. Cartels are defined as private business arrangements to reduce or regulate competition in international trade. Their method of operation, or their usually understood method of operation, takes three farms: first, by agreements, written agreements, and if written agreements are found undesirable, there are oral agreements or, as they are termed in the trade, gentlemen's agreements, if you will; second, by membership in associations, wherein they form associations and limit the membership, as I shall indicate to the house a little later on; and, third, by centralized selling agencies, by which they demand that certain products be sold through a central agency.
Usually they divide a territory so that a member may have a sheltered territory in which he becomes a monopolist. Again, they often place restrictions upon process production, usually by patent agreements. The league of nations report in 1937 stated in part that thirty-two per cent of international trade was controlled by marketing controls; and the United States Department of Justice report in 1939 indicated that there were 179 cartels operating in that country. We in Canada have not escaped from the octopus of monopoly cartelization. As a matter of fact, we all know that every day in every way we are paying tribute to cartels in hundreds of ways.
A few glaring examples I take from the cartel report indicate that farmers are discouraged from mixing their own fertilizers by the fact that the potash and nitrogen cartels keep prices for direct sale to consumers exorbitantly high. Through cartel agreements, the price of sulphur was maintained at SIS a ton for seventeen years and then reduced to $16 a ton which became a new fixed level, and the average profits during this time to the cartel members varied from 13 to 29 per cent. The price of sulphuric acid was forced upward during good times and bad from $12 a ton to $17 a ton, although in a free market the natural tendency is for competition to send prices down. Instead of passing on to consumers the benefits to be had from newer and improved electric light bulbs, General Electric deliberately reduced the life of bulbs from 63260-1944
35 to as much as 62$ per cent, and instead of promoting the use of fluorescent lighting, which is better and cheaper than the old-fashioned bulb, General Electric and Westinghouse agreed to defer the development and marketing of the product as long as possible. A cartel agreement gave the Eddy Match company a virtual monopoly of the domestic market, foreign competition being barred by the policy of the match cartel; and through a cartel controlling plastics, du Pont of America agreed with the I. G. Farben Industries to fix the price of plastic powder for dental use at $45 a pound, although exactly the same product was sold to commercial moulders at 85 cents a pound.
That is the way cartels agree, according to the commissioner, to cripple and hamstring the economy of a country and force the public to pay through the nose for the essentials of life. The Americans have been awake to the situation, and I notice by the Globe and Mail of June 19 that:
The United States Department of Justice has started civil and anti-trust monopoly proceedings against the wealthy International Nickel Company of Canada Limited and its American subsidiary International Nickel Company Incorporated.
From the Globe and Mail of June 28 I see that they have also started proceedings against Electro Metallurgical Company of Canada Limited. But what is more important is a decision which has just been handed down by the United States supreme court dealing with the tobacco trust. I would ask hon. members to pay particular attention to it to see how well it fits into our situation. I quote from the research institute of America of June 14:
A far-reaching decision which can force revision of buying and selling practices in many industries has just been handed down by the supreme court. In a 6-0 ruling involving major tobacco companies the court has extended the revolutionary type of reasoning begun in the Alcoa case. While the earlier decision dealt with the monopoly aspects of a single firm- the new ruling applies virtually the same tests and finds an illegal monopoly where three firms exercised similar controls.
The court makes it clear that actual exclusion of competitors (from interstate or foreign commerce) is not necessary to a finding of unlawful monopoly. It is sufficient if all three of the following conditions occur:
1.	Some members of an industry "combine" to get or keep the power to exclude competitors. The court pointed out that although there was no express agreement among the defenders their action indicated a clear course of dealing. This in itself seemed convincing evidence of a combination or plan to fix and maintain prices and prevent future competitors from getting into the industry.
2.	The group has the "power" to exclude present or future competition from the field. The court noted that the defendants controlled over two-tliirds of the entire domestic cigarette
Combines Investigation

field and over eighty per cent of comparable cigarettes. Following the Alcoa precedent, which uses percentage of control as an index of monopoly power, the court said that "comparative size on this great scale inevitably increased the power of these three to dominate all phases of their industry."
3.	The group "intends" to use this power to maintain a monopoly. Evidence of such intention was found by the court in a wide range sf buying and selling practices of the three companies.
Both combination and intent to exclude competitors were inferred from a wide range of parallel purchasing and sales tactics engaged in by the companies-for example:
(a)	Buying methods. Each of the three majors refused to make any purchases of domestic leaf tobacco unless the other companies were represented on the market. Before markets opened, they placed limitations on the prices which their buyers were permitted to pay and formulated grades so that there frequently was no competition between them. The companies determined in advance of each season what portion of the entire crop each would buy-then spread purchases evenly over the different markets throughout the season. At the time when manufacturers of low-priced cigarettes were beginning to manufacture in quantity, the majors made large purchases of the cheaper leaf needed for the low-priced cigarettes.
(b)	Selling methods. The companies charged identical list prices and gave identical discounts for their cigarettes. They also raised and lowered their prices at the same time. At one point, for example, all three raised their prices on the same date in the face of declining cost and market trends. When the majors were faced with competition from cheaper brands they sold for a while at a loss. Later they insisted that retailers maintain a fixed differential between the quality and the low-priced brands.
RCA observation 1: While no one of these practices taken alone would have been evidence of monopolistic exclusion tactics, the entire pattern is one that could get a group of quasicompetitors into trouble. In this case, for example, fines totalling more than a quarter of a million dollars were imposed.
I point out the steps which our friends to the south of us are taking to deal with this important problem. I have already told the house that in his report Mr. McGregor indicated that cartels restricted production. Restricting production might be beneficial to a cartel, but surely it cannot be beneficial to the economy of this country; for I ask hon. members how restriction of production can ever be socially desirable. It is true the report says that they prevented cyclical fluctuations in prices. As was indicated this afternoon, the aluminum cartel kept prices at fixed levels in good and bad times. I ask hon. members, where is the social advantage if the price is fixed above the average of fluctuating prices which would be permitted in a free economy?
At this particular time we must pay some attention to a problem which arose during the war in order that we might examine the extent
[Mr. Croll.l
to which big firms were able to influence government regulations against the interests of smaller competitors, especially by placing men in key federal agencies. Further, we must examine the degree to which concentration of economic power has increased under war conditions and make certain that we do not permit wartime powers to be used as a cover for anti-social peacetime associations. Individually and collectively the effects of cartel agreements are a bottle-neck in economic progress. After all, what purpose is there to the united nations organization, to the Bretton Woods agreement, to the various trade agreements which we have? If the lifeline between nations, trade relations, is to a great extent under the control of international industrialists; if we are to achieve national unity in this country-and that is our purpose-then we must make sure that wealth is distributed more equally in Canada; that industry is decentralized or in turn compensation is given to the maritimes, to the prairies and to British Columbia for their lack of industries. We must also make sure that the people of the country have an equal standard of living. The only way to do that.is to clear the channels of trade, both domestic and foreign, for we no longer have an agricultural economy in Canada.
We are a great industrial country. A few hours ago an hon. member said that we were the fourth trading nation of the world. Hon. members well know that we are the third largest industrial nation of the world; and if we are left to our own initiative, unshackled and with the know'-how which we have gained during the war, the world is our oyster, particularly when it is realized that we are now reaping the benefits of our price control, of our monetary stability, of our differential in the cost of raw material. To-day we have an advantage over the United States in the markets of the world to the extent of from twenty to thirty per cent. Although we have that advantage we are now starting in to wrestle in public and we shall probably lose the advantage. In the meantime, it seems to me that there is a first-class opportunity to gain some of the markets of the world so long as we are unshackled.
To-night I wish particularly to call attention to an abuse which has crept in, namely, the Canadian Radio Patents Limited, which already has a membership of seventeen and was formed for the purpose of licensing. It is a licensing agency organized by the industry to deal with radio patents. Radios are pretty w'ell standard equipment in Canada. I am told that in Toronto 93 per cent of the homes have radios and 87 per cent in Montreal. I

Combines Investigation
have no doubt that the percentage is just as high throughout the country. To-day radio is an essential to every home, not only for educational purposes but for entertainment and cultural purposes. It is sometimes alleged that it is useful for political purposes. But here is a company having as its objective the prevention of foreign competition and the bolstering of domestic prices; which owns over six hundred radio patents, many of them basic, without which it is impossible to manufacture or sell radios; and which has a financial set-up all its own. They demand from a member $10,000, and at the same time the member must show that he is financially worthy to the extent of $100,000. Even after this has been done, they still have the right to refuse that member admission to the company, on the ground that he has curly hair or pink eyes, or for that matter, on any other ground. To-day, as a result, they are in absolute control of radio patents which are essential for the manufacture of radios in this country. The house may say that we can import radios, but when one realizes that there is a 25 per cent tariff, in addition to the sales tax, excise tax and exchange tax, it will be seen that this is hardly feasible. What is more, under our patent laws, even if a radio is brought into this country, this company have the, rights to charge a royalty on it, and as a matter of fact they have warned many people they would1 do exactly that.
We are getting far away from business as we used to understand it. I remember the time when it was said if you built a better mouse-trap the world would track a path to your door. It seems to me that the people who want to go into the radio business and take their chance ought to be permitted to do so, by paying the ordinary royalties that one pays for the use of patents, basic or otherwise.

I have indicated the evils, which are quite apparent to the house. In the United States they have the Sherman anti-trust law, which to some extent prohibits and at least sets up machinery for the purpose of dealing with trust agreements. Up to the present time Canada has been a bit of a happy hunting ground for cartels; and I think it is undeniable that the time has come for us to make certain that restrictions on production, restrictions on scientific achievement, restrictions on competition in trade, are no longer to be tolerated. As I have pointed out, there is an easily recognized handful of sand being thrown into the machinery. We in this house do not run the machinery,' but we make it possible for the people of Canada to enjoy fully the fruits of their labours.
To me the action to be taken by this house is clear. We must pass an act or acts which will tear down the walls erected by these powerful combines between our factories, our farms, and our markets beyond the seas. We must curb restrictive actions which bar our exports, reduce our national income and cause unemployment in this country. We must maintain full production to meet the needs of our own people, and we must make better use of our natural resources. We have two ways of going about this. We can do something at the international level and we can do something at the domestic level. We are members of the economic and social council of the united nations. We have a representative there. The matter will come before that council for some discussion and action; and it is well that our delegate, whoever he may be, should be instructed as to the action he should take. In so far as this house is concerned, parliament can deal with this matter realistically. Our objectives are good. What we need is a law with teeth. As a matter of fact we have had some experience with cartels. I think most hon. members will remember that when the radium cartel was under the control of the Americans the price was from $100,000 to $170,000 a gram. Then came the Belgians, who reduced the price to $70,000. Then, after discoveries made in the northwest territories in 1938, we brought down the price to $20,000 a gram. Whether that price is fair or unfair I do not know, but it came about as the result of action by this government.
At the present time it seems to me we are merely nibbling at the problem. It is a large problem, a very large one. In the vigorous and tumultuous future it will require more than policing. To fine these companies a quarter of a million dollars, as they do in the United;

This measure goes far; it may work out, but it seems to me that it does not go far enough. A great deal will depend on how it is administered. I am hoping that the Minister of Justice will see that it is administered by such men as Mr. McGregor, in whom we have all confidence, and that he is given adequate facilities and assistance so that when we come back here again, whenever that may be, a report may be presented to this house indicating not only that action has been taken but that results already have been achieved from this legislation. Otherwise we shall feel that we have merely gone through the motions.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
I have listened, as has the house, with great interest to the speeches made this afternoon and this evening, and in particular to the two last hon. gentlemen who spoke. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) clearly showed the existence of a combine in restraint of trade. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) not only read from the report of the inquiry into international cartels and other trade combinations, but added information he himself had gleaned as the result of personal investigation. All who have read this report must be impressed with the fact that to a degree never before known in this country cartels in many commodities and in full restraint of trade have been operating. As a matter of fact it is difficult for me to imagine that anyone could have made a more terrific indictment of the government than is made in the sixty-nine pages of this report made by a commission appointed by the government.
[Mr Croll.)
The commission reports that in regard to various commodities cartels have been continuing in restraint of trade for a good many years and that they are to-day operating. While we are speaking about the subject in this house, the evidence has been secured and put together by a commission to whose chairman high and proper tribute has been paid. The law is on the statute books in the form of section 498 of the criminal code. This section gives wide powers for the laying of informations against any company or individual who unduly limits facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing in any article or commodity which may be a subject of trade or commerce, who restrains or injures trade or commerce in relation to any such article or commodity, or who unduly prevents, limits or lessens the manufacture or production of any such article or commodity, or who unreasonably enhances the price thereof, or who unduly prevents or lessens competition, and certain other matters covered by the section in question.
The Combines Investigation Act was amended in 1935 to permit prosecutions being taken without the necessity of establishing that what was being done was being done in a manner that could be described as unduly. The hon. member for Spadina says that we should put teeth in the law. I see nothing in the amendments before the house at this time that will put any more teeth in the law than exist to-day to prosecute these companies that are acting in restraint of trade for their unlawful actions. The hon. member for Spadina said, and I paraphrase his words, that every day in every way we the people of Canada are paying a tribute to these companies which have taken undue advantage of the people of Canada.
We have had the law up to now. We have had the recommendations and the information contained in this report since October 10, 1945. I ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent): what has the government done since then to punish the wrongdoers who are referred to in the report made by the McGregor commission and who could rightly be convicted of wrongdoing if the statements contained therein are correct? I have looked over the record since 1935 for the purpose of ascertaining just how far this government has gone in carrying out the promises made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the election night of 1935 when he said, or words to this effect, "Now the forces of monopoly and privilege will be shown their place, now the moneyed interests will be brought to task and to account."

Combines Investigation
The McGregor report sets out in detail the existence of cartels in fertilizers, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Spad-ina, in tanning materials, flat glass, sulphur, dyestuffs, tools, titanium pigments, chemicals, electric lamps, radio tubes and so on. The indictment is there. Not only have we the recommendations and the evidence of a commission appointed in Canada; but in the United States, as the result of investigations by the Arnold committee and also of a committee of the United States senate, it has been shown that international cartels exist and have been carrying on their practices in Canada while under indictment in the United States. They have been allowed to remain free and still carry on their nefarious work in this country.
Let me point out what has taken place since 1935. All these cartels have been in existence for ten years or more and yet none has been prosecuted. Here is the record since 1935. An inquiry was made into anthracite coal on February 3, 1937. A combine was reported and proceedings were taken. The anthracite coal importers were fined $48,500. Then on August 31, 1938, a report was made on the distribution of tobacco products in Alberta and elsewhere as being in contravention of the combines act. Prosecutions took place and various tobacco companies were fined. Upon appeal the convictions were set aside on the ground that two offences, one under section 498 of the criminal code and the other under the combines act, were joined together in the one indictment. It strikes me as passing strange that when that conviction was quashed on technical grounds the government has not yet seen its way clear, provided that a combine had been established in connection with these companies, of taking action and proceeding in the courts.
The next report made under this act was with respect to the manufacture and sale of paperboard containers and related products. On March 14, 1939, a combine was reported and prosecutions took place in that year. Fines to the extent of $165,000 were imposed. Finally, on October 31, 1939, wholesale shippers of fruits and vegetables in western Canada were found to be operating a combine in contravention of the act. They were brought before the courts and acquitted. The record shows that proceedings were taken against only small combines in comparison with these international and national combines which are set out particularly in the report of a commission appointed at the instance of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell).
I should like to ascertain from the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) the attitude of the government in Canada in regard to
combines. In October, 1945, there was a meeting in Washington of the Anglo-American financial conference at which the question of cartels was discussed. There was a difference of opinion as between the United Kingdom representatives and the representatives of the United States of America. The Americans proposed, and I quote:
The Americans proposed that a multilateral agreement be concluded among all the major trading nations, and eventually among all others, under which each country would morally commit itself to take whatever steps were necessary to prevent its nationals from entering into combines, etc., in restraint of trade through fixing prices, sharing markets, and similar measures.
The British were prepared to go part way on this thesis. They considered certain cartels were in restraint of trade, but they also felt that others were not. They proposed that efforts should be made to eliminate bad cartels 'out instead of outlawing all cartels, they favoured having a consultative body set up to which a country could complain against a cartel that it considered wras acting in restraint of trade.
I ask the Minister of Justice this:	What
is the attitude of the government of Canada? Does it intend to prevent all cartels and to punish all cartels in restraint of trade? Or does it intend to follow the British practice as suggested by the responsible minister of the British government, that only such cartels should be interfered with as are necessarily illegal?
Before the second reading is over, I think the Minister of Justice should indicate to the house and the country to what extent the companies referred to in the commissioner's report are to be proceeded against. The evidence is here. Mr. McGregor, the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act, places his name on this report, indicating clearly that in his opinion prosecutions should take place. As a matter of fact, as I listened to the hon. member for Spadina referring to electric lamps, these words in the report, at page 22 struck me:
The production of electric lamps in Canada and the United States is largely controlled by the General Electric Company, a United States corporation, which directly or through its subsidiary International General Electric lias agreements with the principal foreign producers (in England, Belgium, Holland, France, Germany, Japan, et cetera) which provide for crosslicensing of patents, exchange of information and allocation of territory. The agreements exclude the foreign producers from the Canadian market, which is reserved for those manufacturers in Canada licensed under Canadian patents, who are likewise barred from exporting to other markets.
Surely any agreement to that effect, to prevent Canadians from importing from another country, is in restraint of trade. The report
goes on:
Combines Investigation

Canadian manufacturers of electric lamps appear to be governed by much the same type of control as to manufacture and sale as has been established by the General Electric Company in the United States. In such an important factor as the length of life, the specifications for lamp construction appear to have been drawn up in the interests of manufacturers. Long life bulbs which have been produced in other countries, in Holland for example, are not permitted to be marketed in Canada.
The report goes on to deal with radio tubes and sets and says:
In its investigation of the radio industry in 1939 and 1940 the tariff board found that Canadian consumers were being unduly exploited through the arrangements then in effect.
There is the report of a body set up by the government, and in order to reinforce its opinion it goes back to 1939 and states that the tariff board at that time found that, in so far as this company was concerned and those associated with it, it was unduly exploiting the Canadian consumer.
Reference has already been made to radio tubes and sets. In the western provinces we find that most of our farmers require a radio as do farmers and other people all over this country. Yet we are unable to get small radios in this country and we are unable to import them. We are denied the opportunity and privilege. The companies in Canada under cartel arrangements are forbidden to manufacture small radios in this country. I will read the particular portion of the report bearing on this, and again I say that this report is an indictment, not of the law as it now stands, but of the government for its failure to act when its responsible representatives and those appointed by it demand that it act. All the action we get in response to that demand is a matter of a few moments, to which particular reference will be made when we go into committee, because we are denied the opportunity of dealing with them on the second reading when only the principle of the bill is at stake. What does this report say about radio tubes and sets? It says:
Arrangements of a like character

Like the arrangements with respect to electric lamps.
-exist with respect to the allocation of world markets for radio sets and radio tubes . . . The arrangements for the exchange of patents and licences protect Canadian manufacturers from outside competition, while the establishment of holding companies to control Canadian patents restricts competition among Canadian licensees.
That is the finding of a responsible committee which was set up under the chairmanship of a -man who has earned the approbation of my hon. friends on all sides of the house and who must have had the evidence before him on which to make findings like that.

I point out now what the radio situation is. Considerable investigation was made of it last January by Mr. Chester Bloom of the press gallery. In an article he sets forth exactly what is happening in this country and explains why people cannot secure the small types of radios. I am going to quote from his words and then I am going to appropriate them as my own. He says:
This patent pool is operated under the name of Thermionics, Ltd. Complaints concerning its operation have been numerous in the past yet no government action has ever been taken to open up the small radio market to free competition.
Is it not fair to interpolate at this moment and ask the government why? There is a demand across this country for small radios. This condition of affairs cannot be explained away as having been in existence only since the war because it dates back to 1935, and possibly even earlier. The fact remains that no consumer in this country has been able to get a small radio. Why? Simply because the things we condemn in the statute are carried on by the companies named in the indictment which is in the form of a commissioner's report. Mr. Chester Bloom goes on to say:
Particularly discriminated against in this respect are farmers who have individual power plants operated by gas engines or wind power. There are some 20,000 such plants on farms in the prairie provinces.
The standard voltage for radios on farms with such individual power service is 32-volt.
Why then, not import such 32-volt radios from the United States?
Then he goes on to state the reason. One reason is that there is a patent pool existent in this country, and the patent pool goes back, he says, to the 1930's. Some might ask, why cannot one write to the United States, buy a radio there, pay the duty on it and bring it in? The answer given by Mr. Bloom is this:
The initial deposit required for an import licence from Thermionics, Ltd. is so high, the importers allege, that it is prohibitive when coupled with the subsequent royalties which must also, of course, be included in the price to the individual purchaser.
That is very much in line with what the hon. member for Spadina said in regard to radio parts in this country.
But suppose-
He says.
-an individual buyer attempts to import such a radio, what happens? He receives at first a tactfully written letter informing him he has fractured the patent laws and is subject to prosecution. If that doesn't suffice, a writ is issued against him. But, according to people who have had this experience, seldom is the case ever taken to court. The writ is merely allowed to stand as an impairment to the credit of the would-be importer . . .

Combines Investigation
There have been instances where Canadian distributors have endeavoured to induce United States radio manufacturers to set up a plant in Canada and manufacture competitive radios in this country. One such manufacturer said frankly he could take all the Canadian market but why should he? He said he would not make any more than he was then with 15 per cent of the Canadian business which he was getting under a gentleman's agreement.
These are not statements loosely made. These are statements reinforced not only by the findings of the McGregor commission but also as a result of the investigations which Mr. McGregor has made over a period of years. But I think we in this house and the country are entitled to find out this: in how many cases did Mr. McGregor or anyone acting on his behalf, since 1935, indicate that there were combines in this country, and in how many cases did prosecutions take place as a result thereof? Because, sir, the position is this: no private individual in this country can take proceedings under the Combines Investigation Act, but only the Attorney General of Canada or, in turn, the attorneys general of the provinces in which the alleged offence has taken place. The result is this, that if the Attorney General of Canada, because, as was pointed out to-day, of the very high costs of taking proceedings, decides not to take proceedings and hands over the ball to the provincial attorney general, do you think it would be reasonable that the province would feel like proceeding with an action when the dominion had decided, apparently, that the cost of prosecution would be so prohibitive that it would not proceed?

But, sir, he says he will not say that, he will accept his responsibility. Then I ask him, why, having regard to what has taken place, and the fact, that there has been a report since October and goodness knows how many reports were sent on to the Department of Justice before October by Mr. McGregor after investigations which he has taken, is it the situation that in a period of eleven years the total number of prosecutions in Canada under the Combines. Investigation Act has been in respect of only four matters?
I should like to ask him too in regard to the international situation. The hon. member for Spadina referred to certain prosecutions which have taken place in the United States. I pointed out one to which I think he made-some reference-the match monopoly. On May 2, 1944, the department of justice of the-United States of America charged ten companies with having contravened the Sherman antitrust act. One of these companies was a Canadian corporation. Those proceedings were gone ahead with, in the United States.. I ask the minister this, is there any collaboration, is there any intercommunication as between the government of the United States and the government of Canada when, as a result of an investigation in the United States it is ascertained that international combines carrying on business in these two countries are operating in- restraint of trade; and, if so, is. there any manner whereby joint prosecutions can take place? Certainly, across the line in the United States large volumes of evidence have been piled up as against two or three corporations operating in Canada, but as yet none of us has heard of any prosecution taking place in this country with regard thereto.
Just one other matter to which, also, reference was made to-day by the hon. member for Spadina, the question of fertilizer. That report is an indictment that affects every farmer in this country either directly or potentially as a possible user of fertilizer. The report reads as follows:
Prices of principal fertilizer materials, potash, nitrogen, and superphosphates, have been controlled under various cartel agreements, some world-wide in extent. The cartels have divided
Combines Investigation

markets and allocated export quotas among members. The resale of potash was deliberately kept high to prevent farmers from mixing theii own fertilizers.
Here, I suggest, is one matter which affects the farmers of this country, and I ask in the very kindest manner possible, what are you going to do about it? My hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) laughs.

speechtext: I said, "in a kindly way".

speechtext:
I appreciate that. Since my hon. friend the Minister of Labour started using that expression "in a kindly way", the atmosphere of this house has improved very greatly, and everybody is using it.
He certainly was the motive power that started the investigation. He is the one who set up this committee and gave it power to act. He has discharged his responsibility. I ask the Minister of Justice, when may parliament and the country expect that in so far as the fertilizer industry is concerned the prosecutions will be taken, to the end that no longer will Canadian farmers be prevented from mixing their own fertilizers by an illegal agreement in restraint of trade and designed with one purpose in mind, to maintain the price at such a height that the largest possible return will come to an international organization?
To-day the Minister of Justice stated that the purpose of the amendments was, if I paraphrase him correctly, to provide the machinery for accelerated action, or, in other words, to provide means whereby prosecutions can be launched and proceeded with, with the greatest possible dispatch. He had the support of every member of this house, and we shall look forward to the acceleration of prosecutions. Certainly no one can characterize in favourable terms the activities of the combines investigation branch of the department since 1935. Of course one of the difficulties has been that Mr. McGregor has had neither the necessary staff nor the necessary appropriations. As I understand it, he is to have a staff of ten experts, and really they are going to set up an organization which is intended to act. I think parliament and the country have the right to know at this time what is to be done when this power of accelerated action has been granted under the amendments asked for under this measure.
As to individual sections, some of these I shall refer to when we come to discuss them in committee. At this time only the question of principle is at stake. I do not see where the new provisions put many teeth in the law as it now stands. To me they look like false

teeth. They are merely the padding of certain sections that can have no effect beyond the effect of the law as it stands at present, because, while they provide new machinery, they do not in any way provide for a change in the nature of the evidence that must be secured in order to found a conviction. In other words, you still have to establish under the criminal code that whatever is done is done unduly. A private individual cannot lay the information. I appeal to the Minister of Justice again. If he desires to secure the power to act, why does he not give the individual consumer, the forgotten man in this country, an opportunity of laying an information under the Combines Investigation Act? As a matter of fact, recommendations have been made in the past to provincial attorneys general that they proceed to prosecute a combine and no prosecution has taken place.
I remember very well, though I speak from memory, that about twenty years ago a potato combine was found to exist in one of the maritime provinces. The matter was turned over to the attorney general of that province and no prosecution took place. The greatest deterrent that any of these corporations can suffer, who are taking undue advantage-and there are only a few of them-is to have publicity given their activities. The greatest police is an aroused public opinion with knowledge and information. When a farmer realizes that he is being unfairly dealt with in the matter of fertilizer, what is the use when he is denied the opportunity of going into a court and himself taking proceedings on the basis of recommendations that have been made by the McGregor commission.
Certainly to-day the situation is such that on the evidence which the McGregor commission has gathered together upon which to found its report, I do not think there would be any great difficulty for an individual having the power to lay the information, to gather together that evidence, having as he would have behind him Mr. McGregor and those associated with him in obtaining the evidence upon which the charges made in the report of the commission were founded.
We can pass laws; but if laws are not enforced they bring the administration into disrepute; they bring justice and fairness and equity into disrepute. We have had the law, and we have had the amendments passed in 1935 to cover some of the abuses that came to light in the price spreads investigation. We have the law; yet with the law at our disposal with a responsible man and a man of experience in charge of the department, with investigations going on and recommendations being made, I say once more that it is not good

Combines Investigation
enough that, with a record such as we find set forth in that report, after eleven years there have been only four prosecutions,-two successful, one reversed on appeal and the other registering an acquittal.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): In closing the debate, I wish first of all to express my gratification at hearing members on all sides of the house pay such a well-deserved tribute to Mr. McGregor, the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act. I am not going to make a political speech, nor am I going to make a speech to try to impress anyone. I brought the bill to parliament because I thought it would enable this house to provide more effective machinery to do something which it is necessary to have done in the public interest, and it is principally with that consideration that I am concerned. It seems to me that this tribute which is being paid to Commissioner McGregor is the best earnest that, if we give Commissioner McGregor the kind of machinery he requires in order to do his job, he will do it and do it in an efficient manner.
I am sure the member for Lake Centre likes to make these indictments upon the government of the day. They probably do provide some headlines; they do provide some passing interest. But it does not last very long, and the hon. member and I know that what really counts is what is done, rather than what is said.

LAURENT: He was in the senate; it was in the senate that this was introduced; and it came here the day before the last of the session and had to be taken in that form or nothing at all would have been obtained. The hon. member knows that would be something of little substantial effect. He pointed out in his speech that there are very few individuals who are going to undertake, at their own risk and at their own expense, a long struggle with a powerful corporation to establish that its manner of doing its business is illegal. But there will be no objection to having the law framed in such a manner that if such a courageous, public-spirited citizen wishes to do it on his own account he will be privileged to do so. He already has had the right to do so under section 498 or 498A of the code.
The matter to which the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) referred is one which, on the facts stated in the brief he submitted, would clearly constitute a violation of section 498A of the code. It is a matter which is being carefully investigated by Mr. McGregor. Mr. McGregor has not yet come to the conclusion that he should recommend that proceedings be instituted, but he has had the matter under consideration. He has had correspondence with the interested parties and is giving it serious attention. But apparently Merchants Consolidated Limited, made up of four hundred individual merchants, would prefer to have the government undertake the risk and expense of bringing Canadian Industries Limited to time than do it itself.
With respect to international cartels, the hon. member for Lake Centre knows, as I know, that we cannot prosecute for offences committed in foreign parts; that arrangements
Combines Investigation

to that end have to be negotiated internationally, and the matter is on the agenda of the meeting called originally by the United States government and which has now been placed under the aegis of the economic and social council of the united nations. Joint action is required there. We cannot prosecute anyone here in Canada because he has to charge for the components of fertilizer which he imports into this country a price which gives him some margin over the laid-down cost at the Canadian port of entry. That is something which we cannot effectively deal with here. We can refuse to take these component parts at all, but that would not give us the fertilizer. It so happens that, in spite of the serious situation disclosed in this report of the commissioner on cartels, we still prefer to have the fertilizer at the price we have to pay than to do without it. But the purpose served by making these facts public is to prepare the way for the international agreements we hope to be able to make which will bring about by international action the curbing of such activities.
Here we are asking for amendments to the legislation which appear to be necessary to enable the commission, as it is being reorganized, to function in an efficient manner. During the war there were price ceilings which afforded some protection. It is known to members of the house that the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act was on loan to the wartime prices and trade board and was, up to a few months ago, in charge of the enforcement of the regulations of that board. Since the beginning of the year he has returned to his former job of giving his time and attention to the matters to which the Combines Investigation Act applies. I think most hon. members have in him the confidence which was expressed by those who have taken part in the debate, and they believe that if he is given the statutory legislation he requires, and is not hampered in his operations, he will do an efficient job.
I can say to the hon. member for Lake Centre that there have been no reports from the commissioner to the Department of Justice not acted upon, and I am informed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) that since 1939 there were no reports to the Minister of Labour from the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act which were not acted upon.
While this act is administered under the Department of Justice and I happen to be there I can give the house the assurance that the efforts of the commissioner will be fully seconded in every possible way to eliminate, to the extent to which it may be feasible, the

detrimental effects of these monopolies, trusts and cartels referred to in his report. Existence of an alleged combine in the distribution of tobacco products in the province of Alberta and elsewhere in Canada was reported by the commissioner in August, 1938, after an investigation commenced in March, 1938. A system of price-fixing agreements, stop-lists, boycotts andl related trade restrictions operating to the detriment of the public was reported to have been put into effect in Alberta and other provinces by certain, tobacco manufacturers and wholesalers. Prosecution proceedings instituted in Alberta in 1938 under section 498 of the criminal code subsequently were stayed by the crown and charges were laid for offences under the Combines Investigation Act. Thirty-six companies and individuals engaged in the tobacco business,

Combines Investigation
including wholesalers and seven, manufacturers, were convicted by a jury at Edmonton in July, 1941, of offences of participation in a combination to fix and enhance prices of tobacco products and operation of a merger, trust or monopoly substantially controlling tobacco distribution throughout Canada to the detriment of the public.
