I do not wish to press this unnecessarily, but I am surprised at the explanation given the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard regarding the circumstances connected with the decision made that no further proceedings would be taken against these tobacco companies. They were charged with having in 1938 and previously done many acts in restraint of trade, having indulged in unfair practices. According to the minister there was justification for the charge; because, if I understood him rightly, the evidence was to that effect. He said that the reason they did not proceed against them after they got away on technical grounds in the court of appeal on another charge was that the wartime prices and trade board was operating then and that, therefore, there was no danger of these companies taking advantage any more. In any event, they reduced their prices by ten per cent. What it amounts to, therefore, is this, that they were not proceeded against any more, after having won a new trial in the court of appeal on a technical ground, and they were not proceeded against because they said they would not do wrong any more; or the attitude of the authorities was, "They cannot do wrong any more because of the action of the wartime prices and trade board." Section 3 is the only part of the amending bill which makes any reference at all to the conclusions of the McGregor report. Section 3 permits the commissioner to compile further information with regard to monopolistic conditions arising either from the operations of international cartels or otherwise. I should like to know, first of all, whether any further investigations are being made along any particular channels which have not been explored by the McGregor commission and whether there is an appropriation and a staff to give effect to this new section. Why does this bill not contain some measure to control international cartels? Either on second reading or after we got into committee I understood the minister to say that until some international agreement was reached with other nations it would be impossible to deal with the Canadian sections of international cartels. I cannot understand why the new section 30 and the old section 2 cannot be made applicable at the present time to international cartels. If so, I should like to know whether proceedings implementing the McGregor report are being taken under these sections.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: We have not yet come to section 30. Section 30 is being asked for precisely for the purpose of enabling the commissioner to deal in Canada with that part of an international cartel arrangement which would operate here. As to providing in this bill curbs or provisions to implement international agreements with respect to cartels, we were not able to devise anything which would have been other than a provision empowering the governor in council to take such action as might be required to carry out an international agreement. I felt that I
would not ask parliament to empower the governor in council to do that; that parliament would probably want to know what the agreement was before it would give authority to implement it. Even if it did take a little more time, it was better to wait until we had the agreement and then come to parliament and ask parliament to provide for it to be implemented instead of asking for a blanket authority in advance to carry out such agreement as might be arrived at. My experience at the last session of parliament made me feel it was better not to ask parliament for such blanket authority, even if it did involve taking a little more time to accomplish our purpose.

I think we are better off with the expression "international cartel", because we know what we have in mind; whilst if we set up a definition there would be a form of arrangement arrived at which would not be within the terms of the definition.

As the minister knows, the economic and social council of the united nations, to which some reference has already been made in this debate, has some powers which could hardly be described as having very sharp teeth. That council, of course, is set up for the purpose of initiating studies, making recommendations and so on; but there are no operative provisions in regard to enforcement or anything of that kind. From what the minister says, I take it that there is in contemplation some sort of international agreement with respect to the question of international cartels. Will that agreement be initiated or entered into under the aegis of the economic and social council, or will it be a separate agreement among certain nations particularly interested in the subject?

Mr. ST. LAURENT: My understanding is that the United States government put out its proposals for expansion of world trade and employment; that those proposals had been communicated to several governments and had been given tentative approval; that at the general assembly of the united nations a decision was made that the social and economic council would take the responsibility of convening this meeting of the nations to discuss the proposals put forth by the United States government, which among others contained proposals for the elimination of cartels; and that it is hoped the governments participating in the conference would agree upon terms to eliminate these international cartels or to control them in such a manner as to prevent their harmful effects upon the economies of the participating nations.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS- COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
It seemed to me that unless there was some agreement among the governments interested in the suppression or control of the cartel situation at the international level, two things might result which would be prejudicial to our national organization as well as to the international organization. That is, if we allow in the world some superauthority which is seemingly beyond the power of governments themselves to control, as international cartels at certain stages actually seem to be; if that condition were allowed to continue it would seriously affect the international organization which has been set up, and, in addition, would weaken the position of our own government and our own parliament in dealing with that matter at the domestic level. The evidence clearly shows that at various stages these international cartels weave themselves into the very fabric of our own domestic situation and our own economic structure; and I should fancy that one of the principal advantages in the reform of cartels would be to see that international cartels are dealt with at that level in the manner in which they should be dealt with. In other words, there should be no higher authority and no higher power than the government which represents the people of a nation, though there seems to have been some evidence in the past, in any event, that governments have been unable to cope with a situation having so many international ramifications that it almost overpowers governments which are supposed to represent the people themselves.
I make these remarks only because I wanted the point clarified with respect to the part played by the economic and social council. If the matter is to be simply left to that council, certainly under the united nations charter the

Questions
council has not sufficient power to enable it to do anything in connection with cartels except to initiate studies and make recommendations. If, however, at the world trade conference a proper agreement is reached, of course that alters the picture entirely, so that eventually we may hope for some teeth in the procedure for dealing with this affair on an international basis.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	I am sure there will
be no difference of view between the government of the United States and the government of the United Kingdom as to the desirability of there being no commercial or industrial power greater than the power of governments to determine what the economy of the respective nations should be.
